20. Exchange Rates and International Finance

Learning goals

Chapter 19 studied trade between countries. This chapter adds the price at which their currencies trade, the exchange rate, and asks what moves it in the long run and in the short run. By the end of it you will be able to:

  • tell the nominal exchange rate (the price of a currency) from the real exchange rate (the price of goods), and derive the long-run exchange rate from the law of one price and the quantity theory, in levels and in growth rates (purchasing power parity), and the drift of real exchange rates (Balassa-Samuelson);
  • derive uncovered interest parity and use it to explain why the exchange rate jumps with interest rates and why a fixed exchange rate ties a country’s interest rate to the rest of the world;
  • test the law of one price on data: the yen and the dollar since 1971, and the Big Mac index;
  • derive the open-economy IS curve and the AD curve, read their comparative statics (a flatter IS curve, a rise in foreign interest rates as an aggregate demand shock), and solve the AS/AD dynamics that follow;
  • explain the policy trilemma and read the history of exchange-rate regimes, currency crises and the euro crisis in the data;
  • in Python: build price levels from inflation rates with cumprod, plot two vertical scales in one figure, switch views with Plotly buttons, rebase an index, and reshape tables with melt;
  • go beyond the textbook’s countries: pick any of up to 200 economies from a list (SelectMultiple), filter rows with isin, compare data from the World Bank, the IMF, the OECD and the Penn World Table, and spot gaps, breaks and differences in definitions.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

The data figures can show many countries. On the website they use the helpers below: a legend you can click, a slider that changes the data of every line at once, and a menu of country groups.

Show the helper code 
# @title Helpers for the many-country website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def compact(y):
    """Round to 4 significant digits, so that the saved figure stays small."""
    return [None if v is None or v != v else float(f"{v:.4g}") for v in y]


def slim(trace):
    """Make a line smaller: rounded y, and the hover label from the trace name instead of one text per point."""
    trace.y = compact(trace.y)
    if trace.hovertext is not None and len(trace.hovertext) > 0 and trace.hovertext[0] == trace.name:
        trace.hovertext = None
        trace.hovertemplate = trace.hovertemplate.replace("%{hovertext}", "%{fullData.name}")
    return trace


def legend_only(fig, keep):
    """Show the traces named in keep; list the others in the legend only, so a click adds them."""
    for trace in fig.data:
        trace.visible = True if trace.name in keep else "legendonly"
        slim(trace)
    return fig


def data_slider(make_figure, name, values, start, title, label=None, **fixed):
    """A slider whose steps replace the y data of every line (matched by name), so legend clicks are kept.

    Lines missing at the start value are added empty. title is a text with {} where the slider value goes."""
    figures = {v: make_figure(**{name: v}, **fixed) for v in values}
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[start].layout)
    for v in [start] + list(values):
        for t in figures[v].data:
            if t.name not in [u.name for u in fig.data]:
                t.y = t.y if v == start else [None] * len(t.y)
                fig.add_trace(slim(t))
    steps = []
    for v in values:
        ys = {t.name: compact(t.y) for t in figures[v].data}
        new_y = [ys.get(t.name, [None] * len(t.y)) for t in fig.data]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(v), args=[{"y": new_y}, {"title.text": title.format(v)}]))
    fig.update_layout(title=title.format(start), sliders=[dict(
        active=values.index(start), steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60), currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

def country_groups(names, book, book_label, regions=True):
    """Groups for the website menus: the textbook's countries, G7, euro area, large emerging, World Bank regions."""
    info = country_info[country_info.country.isin(names)]
    euro = list(info[info.euro_since.notna() | (info.country == "Euro area")].country)

# @title Helper: a figure with a menu of country groups (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def menu_figure(make_figure, options, categories=False):
    """Precompute make_figure for every menu option and join the figures with a dropdown menu.

    options maps each menu label to a list of countries, or to a dict of keyword arguments.
    With categories=True (bar charts) each option also sets the order and the range of the x-axis."""
    labels = list(options)
    figures = [make_figure(**options[g]) if isinstance(options[g], dict) else make_figure(tuple(options[g]))
               for g in labels]
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[0].layout)
    owner = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == 0)
            fig.add_trace(slim(trace))
            owner.append(i)
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title.text": f.layout.title.text, "yaxis.type": f.layout.yaxis.type or "linear",
                  "yaxis.range": f.layout.yaxis.range, "yaxis.tickvals": f.layout.yaxis.tickvals,
                  "yaxis.autorange": f.layout.yaxis.range is None,
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes],
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations]}
        if categories:
            names = list(dict.fromkeys(x for t in f.data for x in t.x))
            layout.update({"xaxis.categoryorder": "array", "xaxis.categoryarray": names,
                           "xaxis.range": [-0.5, len(names) - 0.5]})
            if i == 0:
                fig.update_xaxes(categoryorder="array", categoryarray=names, range=[-0.5, len(names) - 0.5])
        buttons.append(dict(label=labels[i], method="update", args=[{"visible": [o == i for o in owner]}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(t=110), updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=0, x=0, y=1.02,
                                                            xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom")])
    return fig

Model overview

An exchange rate is a price: how much of another country’s money one dollar buys. This chapter studies that price over two horizons. In the long run, a good should cost about the same everywhere once its prices are written in one currency, so the exchange rate follows the price levels of the two countries, and a country with more inflation ends up with a weaker currency. In the short run, prices hardly move, and the exchange rate jumps with interest rates instead: when U.S. interest rates rise, investors want dollars, the dollar gets stronger and U.S. goods become harder to sell abroad.

That second link brings trade into the short-run model of earlier chapters. Net exports now fall when the interest rate rises, just like investment, and a change in foreign interest rates becomes a demand shock at home. This section builds the chapter’s models one block at a time, each from its assumptions to its predictions: the law of one price and purchasing power parity, in levels and in growth rates; the Balassa-Samuelson effect, which explains why real exchange rates drift; uncovered interest parity, which links exchange rates to interest rates; fixed exchange rates and the policy trilemma; the open-economy IS curve; the open economy in the AS/AD model; and the simple arithmetic behind the euro crisis. At the end, ### The model in code turns the key results into Python functions and checks each of them with numbers.

Notation. A bar over a letter marks a parameter, set outside the model, such as \(\bar{b}_{nx}\) or the foreign real interest rate \(\bar{R}^w\). As in the book, a bar over a price or an exchange rate, such as \(\bar{E}\), marks its long-run value. A superscript \(w\) (“world”) marks the foreign country, or the rest of the world. Growth rates are written \(g\), so \(g_E\) is the growth rate of the exchange rate, and \(\pi\) is inflation, the growth rate of the price level.

Exchange rates in the long run: the law of one price and PPP

Assumptions

1. The exchange rate. \(E\) is the nominal exchange rate: how much foreign money one dollar buys, for example 0.92 euros per dollar. It is the price of a dollar. When \(E\) rises, a dollar buys more foreign money: the dollar appreciates. When \(E\) falls, it depreciates.

2. Arbitrage in goods. If the same good were cheaper in one country than in another, traders would buy it where it is cheap and ship it to where it is dear, until the gap disappears. In the long run this leaves the law of one price: a good costs the same in every country, once its prices are written in one currency. With \(P\) the price in the United States (in dollars) and \(P^w\) the price abroad (in foreign currency),

\[EP = P^w. \tag{1}\]

The left side turns the U.S. price into foreign money. The units show it: \(E\) is euros per dollar and \(P\) is dollars per chip, so their product is euros per chip, the same unit as \(P^w\). Transport costs, tariffs and taxes can keep the two sides apart, but only by about the size of those frictions.

3. Price levels come from money. Apply equation (1) to the whole basket of goods of each economy, so that \(P\) and \(P^w\) are the two price levels. In the long run each price level follows from the quantity theory of money (Chapter 8): \(M_tV_t = P_tY_t\), with constant velocity \(\bar{V}\) and output at potential \(\bar{Y}\), so \(\bar{P} = \bar{M}\bar{V}/\bar{Y}\), and in the same way abroad, \(\bar{P}^w = \bar{M}^w\bar{V}^w/\bar{Y}^w\).

Solving the model

Step 1: the long-run nominal exchange rate. The quantity theory fixes the two price levels, so only \(E\) is left free in equation (1). Divide both sides by \(\bar{P}\):

\[\bar{E} = \frac{\bar{P}^w}{\bar{P}}. \tag{2}\]

The units work: euros per good divided by dollars per good is euros per dollar, because “per good” cancels.

Intuition. A dollar is worth what it buys. If a basket costs 100 dollars in the United States and 92 euros in Germany, then 100 dollars and 92 euros are worth the same, and a dollar is worth 0.92 euros.

Step 2: money and the exchange rate. Substitute the two quantity-theory price levels into equation (2):

\[\bar{E} = \frac{\bar{M}^w\bar{V}^w/\bar{Y}^w}{\bar{M}\bar{V}/\bar{Y}} = \frac{\bar{M}^w}{\bar{M}}\times\frac{\bar{V}^w}{\bar{V}}\times\frac{\bar{Y}}{\bar{Y}^w}.\]

Taking logs turns the products into sums (Appendix C.4):

\[\ln\bar{E} = (\ln\bar{M}^w - \ln\bar{M}) + (\ln\bar{V}^w - \ln\bar{V}) + (\ln\bar{Y} - \ln\bar{Y}^w).\]

Each coefficient is \(+1\) or \(-1\), so each is an elasticity of size one. Doubling the number of dollars doubles U.S. prices and halves the long-run value of the dollar. In the long run the exchange rate is the relative price of two piles of paper money.

Step 3: pricing goods instead of currencies. The real exchange rate measures what one U.S. good costs in units of foreign goods:

\[RER \equiv \frac{EP}{P^w}, \qquad \text{in units}\quad \frac{\text{euros}}{\text{dollar}}\times\frac{\text{dollars}}{\text{U.S. good}}\times\frac{\text{foreign good}}{\text{euros}} = \frac{\text{foreign goods}}{\text{U.S. good}}.\]

The nominal rate is the price at which two currencies trade; the real rate is the price at which two countries’ goods trade. Equation (1) says that \(EP\) and \(P^w\) are equal in the long run, so their ratio is one:

\[\overline{RER} = \frac{\bar{E}\bar{P}}{\bar{P}^w} = 1. \tag{3}\]

Step 4: purchasing power parity in growth rates. Equation (2) is also called purchasing power parity (PPP). To see how it moves over time, take logs, \(\ln\bar{E}_t = \ln\bar{P}^w_t - \ln\bar{P}_t\), and subtract the same equation one year earlier. The change in the log of a variable is approximately its growth rate (Appendix C.5), and the growth rate of a price level is inflation:

\[\underbrace{\ln\bar{E}_t - \ln\bar{E}_{t-1}}_{\approx\, g_E} = \underbrace{(\ln\bar{P}^w_t - \ln\bar{P}^w_{t-1})}_{\approx\,\pi^w} - \underbrace{(\ln\bar{P}_t - \ln\bar{P}_{t-1})}_{\approx\,\pi},\]

so that

\[g_E \approx \pi^w - \pi. \tag{4}\]

This is the growth rule for a ratio, \(g_{X/Z} = g_X - g_Z\). The exact yearly version is \(\bar{E}_t/\bar{E}_{t-1} = (1+\pi^w)/(1+\pi)\). With the quantity theory and constant velocities, inflation is money growth minus output growth (Chapter 8), \(\pi = g_M - g_Y\), so equation (4) also reads \(g_E \approx (g_{M^w} - g_{Y^w}) - (g_M - g_Y)\).

Intuition. The currency of the country with more inflation loses value, at a yearly rate equal to the inflation gap. If U.S. prices rise by 4 percent a year and Japanese prices by 2 percent, the dollar should buy about 2 percent fewer yen each year. After 25 years that adds up to a fall of about 40 percent, since \((1.02/1.04)^{25} \approx 0.62\).

Step 5: the real exchange rate in growth rates. Take logs of the definition in step 3 in the same way. The growth rate of a product is the sum of the growth rates, and that of a ratio is the difference:

\[g_{RER} \approx g_E + \pi - \pi^w. \tag{5}\]

If PPP holds, equation (4) makes the right side zero and the real exchange rate stays at one. When the real exchange rate does change, either the nominal rate moved more than the inflation gap, or prices moved while the nominal rate stayed put. Fig. 3 uses equation (5) to build Japan’s real exchange rate from the data.

What the model predicts

A permanent 1% rise in … changes \(\bar{E}\) (foreign currency per dollar) by because
U.S. money \(\bar{M}\) \(-1\%\) U.S. prices rise 1%
foreign money \(\bar{M}^w\) \(+1\%\) foreign prices rise 1%
U.S. output \(\bar{Y}\) \(+1\%\) U.S. prices fall 1%
U.S. velocity \(\bar{V}\) \(-1\%\) U.S. prices rise 1%
any of them \(0\) for \(\overline{RER}\) the long-run real exchange rate is always one
  • More inflation, weaker currency. A dollar that depreciates against the yen for decades, as in Fig. 1, requires U.S. inflation above Japanese inflation (equation 4). Fig. 2 checks this.
  • The level of the nominal rate has no meaning of its own. A new currency worth 1,000 old ones changes \(\bar{E}\) a thousandfold and leaves the real exchange rate, and every real variable, untouched: the classical dichotomy of the long run.
  • The law holds only roughly. It needs goods that can be shipped. The next block explains why prices of goods that cannot be shipped make real exchange rates drift.

Why real exchange rates drift: the Balassa-Samuelson effect

This block writes the book’s verbal explanation of the Balassa-Samuelson effect as a small model, in our own notation.

Assumptions

  1. Each economy has a traded sector (cars, phones) and a nontraded sector (haircuts, restaurant meals). Output per worker is \(A_T\) in the traded sector and \(A_N\) in the nontraded sector, and abroad \(A^w_T\) and \(A^w_N\).
  2. Workers move freely between the two sectors of their own country, so both sectors pay the same wage \(W\). Firms are competitive, so the wage equals the value of what a worker produces: \(W = P_TA_T = P_NA_N\).
  3. The law of one price, equation (1), holds for traded goods only: \(EP_T = P^w_T\).
  4. The price level is an average of the two prices with weight \(\theta\) on traded goods, \(P = P_T^{\theta}P_N^{1-\theta}\), and in the same way abroad.

Solving the model

Step 1: the price of nontraded goods. From \(P_TA_T = P_NA_N\), divide by \(A_N\):

\[P_N = P_T\,\frac{A_T}{A_N}.\]

A haircut costs more where the barber could have earned more in a factory.

Step 2: the price level. Substitute \(P_N\) into the price level and use the exponent rule \(x^{\theta}x^{1-\theta} = x\) (Appendix C.3):

\[P = P_T^{\theta}\left(P_T\frac{A_T}{A_N}\right)^{1-\theta} = P_T^{\theta}P_T^{1-\theta}\left(\frac{A_T}{A_N}\right)^{1-\theta} = P_T\left(\frac{A_T}{A_N}\right)^{1-\theta}.\]

Step 3: the real exchange rate. Write the same expression abroad and form \(EP/P^w\). The traded-goods part is \(EP_T/P^w_T = 1\) by assumption 3, so

\[RER = \frac{EP_T}{P^w_T}\times\left(\frac{A_T/A_N}{A^w_T/A^w_N}\right)^{1-\theta} = \left(\frac{A_T/A_N}{A^w_T/A^w_N}\right)^{1-\theta}. \tag{6}\]

In growth rates, by the rules for powers and ratios, \(g_{RER} = (1-\theta)\left[(g_{A_T} - g_{A_N}) - (g_{A^w_T} - g_{A^w_N})\right]\).

Intuition. Fast productivity growth in factories raises wages throughout the economy. Factory goods do not get dearer, because they compete with the world, but services do, because their productivity grows slowly while their wage bill rises. A country whose traded-goods productivity grows faster than abroad sees its price level, and so its real exchange rate, rise.

What the model predicts

  • Growing economies appreciate in real terms. With \(\theta = 1/2\), a country whose traded-sector productivity grows 3 points a year faster than the other country’s (relative to services) sees its real exchange rate rise by about \(1.5\%\) a year, or by a factor of \(1.015^{24} \approx 1.43\) over 24 years. Japan’s real exchange rate rose in this way while it caught up, until 1995 (Fig. 3).
  • Rich countries look expensive. At a point in time, rich countries have a high \(A_T/A_N\), and so dearer services and a higher price level. A Big Mac includes the cook’s wage and the rent of the restaurant, so it should cost more in rich countries. The Big Mac section after Fig. 3 tests this.
  • The effect works through relative productivities, not through money, so it can last for decades without any violation of the law of one price for traded goods.

Exchange rates in the short run: uncovered interest parity

The book argues in words that a higher U.S. interest rate makes the dollar stronger. This block states that argument as an equation, uncovered interest parity (UIP), a standard tool of international finance.

Assumptions

  1. Sticky prices. In the short run \(P\) and \(P^w\) hardly move, as with the sticky inflation of the short-run model.
  2. Free financial flows. Investors can hold U.S. bonds, which pay the nominal interest rate \(i_t\) in dollars, or foreign bonds, which pay \(i^w\) in foreign currency. They care only about the expected return and ignore risk.
  3. An anchor for the future. Investors expect the exchange rate to be \(E^e_{t+1}\) next year. Because the long run is pinned down by PPP, equation (2), we take this expectation as given when the interest rate changes.

Solving the model

Step 1: two ways to invest a dollar. Kept in the United States, one dollar grows to \(1 + i_t\) dollars in a year. Sent abroad, it is first changed into \(E_t\) units of foreign currency, which grow to \(E_t(1+i^w)\), and are then changed back at the expected rate \(E^e_{t+1}\), giving \(E_t(1+i^w)/E^e_{t+1}\) dollars. If one route paid more, money would flow into it until the two expected returns were equal:

\[1 + i_t = (1+i^w)\,\frac{E_t}{E^e_{t+1}}. \tag{7}\]

Step 2: solve for today’s exchange rate. Multiply both sides by \(E^e_{t+1}\) and divide by \(1+i^w\):

\[E_t = E^e_{t+1}\times\frac{1+i_t}{1+i^w}.\]

Take logs and use the approximation \(\ln(1+x) \approx x\) for small \(x\) (Appendix C.6): \(\ln E_t \approx \ln E^e_{t+1} + (i_t - i^w)\). If the interest gap is expected to last \(n\) years before the exchange rate returns to its anchor \(E^e_{t+n}\), the same steps applied \(n\) times give \(E_t = E^e_{t+n}\left[(1+i_t)/(1+i^w)\right]^n\), so that

\[\ln E_t \approx \ln E^e_{t+n} + n\,(i_t - i^w). \tag{8}\]

A rise in the U.S. interest rate by 1 point, with \(i^w\) and the anchor unchanged, makes the dollar jump up today by about \(n\) percent. The policy-trilemma model of Fig. 7 uses a jump of 5 percent per point, which corresponds to an interest gap expected to last about 5 years.

Step 3: what happens after the jump. Rearrange equation (7) as \(E^e_{t+1}/E_t = (1+i^w)/(1+i_t)\). In logs, the expected growth rate of \(E\) is \(g^e_E \approx i^w - i_t\). When U.S. bonds pay more, the dollar must be expected to lose value from now on, by exactly the interest gap, so that holding dollars is no better than holding euros. The only way to get both a higher interest rate and an expected depreciation is for the dollar to jump up at once and then slide back.

Step 4: what sticky prices do to the real rate. With sticky prices, \(\pi\) and \(\pi^w\) are close to zero over a few weeks, so equation (5) gives \(g_{RER} \approx g_E\). Every surprise move in \(E\) becomes a move in the real exchange rate. With sticky inflation, a higher nominal rate \(i_t\) also means a higher real rate \(R_t = i_t - \pi^e_t\) (the Fisher equation), so the same chain runs from the real interest rate:

\[\uparrow R_t \;\Rightarrow\; \uparrow E_t \;\Rightarrow\; \uparrow \frac{E_tP}{P^w}.\]

What the model predicts

Change Effect on \(E_t\) today Effect on the real exchange rate
U.S. interest rate \(i_t\) up 1 point up about \(n\) percent (dollar appreciates) up by the same percent
foreign interest rate \(i^w\) up 1 point down about \(n\) percent (dollar depreciates) down by the same percent
expected future rate \(E^e\) up 1% up 1% (elasticity one) up 1%
Long run Short run
nominal exchange rate \(E\) relative price levels, PPP (equation 2) interest rates and expectations, UIP (equation 8)
real exchange rate \(EP/P^w\) equal to one (equation 3) moves with \(E\), because prices are sticky

Fixed exchange rates and the policy trilemma

Assumptions

  1. The central bank promises to trade its currency at a fixed rate \(E_{fix}\), for example 1 Argentine peso per dollar, and holds foreign exchange reserves to keep that promise.
  2. Investors believe the promise, so they expect the rate to stay where it is: \(E^e_{t+1} = E_t = E_{fix}\).
  3. Financial flows are free, so uncovered interest parity, equation (7), holds.

Solving the model

Step 1: the interest rate is no longer free. Put \(E_t = E^e_{t+1}\) into equation (7). The ratio \(E_t/E^e_{t+1}\) equals one, so

\[i_t = i^w. \tag{9}\]

A country that fixes its exchange rate and keeps its financial markets open must set the same interest rate as the country it pegs to. When the Federal Reserve raises its rate, the central bank of Argentina must follow, whatever the state of its own economy.

Step 2: prices are no longer free either. In the long run, equation (2) with \(\bar{E} = E_{fix}\) gives \(\bar{P} = \bar{P}^w/E_{fix}\): the price level at home must move one for one with the price level abroad, and equation (4) with \(g_E = 0\) gives \(\pi = \pi^w\). By the quantity theory, money growth at home must match money growth abroad (adjusted for output growth). This is why a peg can import a trusted central bank, and also why it fails when the government needs to print money to pay its bills (Chapter 8).

Step 3: the gold standard is a law of one price for gold. Under the gold standard each country fixed the price of an ounce of gold in its own money: \(P^{gold}\) dollars in the United States, \(P^{gold,w}\) pounds in Britain. Apply equation (2) to gold alone: \(E = P^{gold,w}/P^{gold}\) pounds per dollar. Fig. 6 computes this gold parity.

Step 4: a peg that markets doubt. Suppose investors start to fear a devaluation and expect \(E^e_{t+1}\) below \(E_{fix}\). Solve equation (7) for the interest rate:

\[1 + i_t = (1+i^w)\,\frac{E_{fix}}{E^e_{t+1}}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad i_t \approx i^w + \text{expected percent depreciation}.\]

With \(i^w = 5\) percent, an expected devaluation of 10 percent requires \(i_t = 1.05/0.90 - 1 \approx 16.7\) percent to keep investors holding the currency. If the central bank does not raise its rate that far, investors sell the currency for reserves; when the reserves run out, the peg breaks, as in Mexico in 1994, Asia in 1997 and Argentina in 2002 (Fig. 8).

What the model predicts

UIP links three things: the exchange rate, the domestic interest rate, and the freedom of money to cross borders. Fixing any two of them determines the third, which is the policy trilemma of Fig. 7:

Regime (side of the triangle) Keeps Gives up Why, in equations
floating rate (United States) monetary autonomy, free flows a stable exchange rate \(i_t\) is chosen freely, so \(E_t\) moves with \(i_t - i^w\) (equation 8)
currency board or monetary union (Argentina 1991–2001, the euro) a stable rate, free flows monetary autonomy \(E_t\) fixed and UIP hold, so \(i_t = i^w\) (equation 9)
capital controls (China 1996–2005) a stable rate, monetary autonomy free flows \(i_t \neq i^w\) with \(E\) fixed breaks UIP, so trading in the currency must be rationed

The open-economy IS curve

Assumptions

  1. Net exports and the real exchange rate. When U.S. goods are expensive relative to foreign goods (a high real exchange rate), exports are low and imports high, so net exports \(NX \equiv EX - IM\) are low.
  2. The exchange-rate channel. By the UIP block, the real exchange rate rises when the U.S. real interest rate \(R_t\) rises and falls when the foreign real interest rate \(\bar{R}^w\) rises. Together, assumptions 1 and 2 make net exports, as a share of potential output, fall with the gap between the two real interest rates:

\[\frac{NX_t}{\bar{Y}_t} = \bar{a}_{nx} - \bar{b}_{nx}\,(R_t - \bar{R}^w). \tag{10}\]

\(\bar{a}_{nx}\) is the medium-run trade balance and \(\bar{b}_{nx} > 0\) measures how strongly trade reacts to the interest gap. With \(\bar{b}_{nx} = 0\) we are back in the closed-economy IS curve of Chapter 11. 3. The rest of the IS curve is unchanged (Chapter 11): \(C_t/\bar{Y}_t = \bar{a}_c\), \(G_t/\bar{Y}_t = \bar{a}_g\), \(I_t/\bar{Y}_t = \bar{a}_i - \bar{b}_i(R_t - \bar{r})\), where \(\bar{r}\) is the marginal product of capital; and output is spent, \(Y_t = C_t + I_t + G_t + NX_t\). Short-run output is \(\tilde{Y}_t \equiv (Y_t - \bar{Y}_t)/\bar{Y}_t\).

Solving the model

Step 1: add and subtract \(\bar{r}\). Investment depends on \(R_t - \bar{r}\), but net exports on \(R_t - \bar{R}^w\). Write \(R_t - \bar{R}^w = (R_t - \bar{r}) - (\bar{R}^w - \bar{r})\) and multiply out:

\[\frac{NX_t}{\bar{Y}_t} = \bar{a}_{nx} - \bar{b}_{nx}(R_t - \bar{r}) + \bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r}).\]

Nothing has changed: the two \(\bar{r}\) terms cancel. But now trade depends on the same gap as investment, plus a term that only the rest of the world can move.

Step 2: divide spending by potential output. Divide \(Y_t = C_t + I_t + G_t + NX_t\) by \(\bar{Y}_t\) and substitute each share:

\[\frac{Y_t}{\bar{Y}_t} = \bar{a}_c + \left[\bar{a}_i - \bar{b}_i(R_t - \bar{r})\right] + \bar{a}_g + \left[\bar{a}_{nx} - \bar{b}_{nx}(R_t - \bar{r}) + \bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r})\right].\]

Step 3: collect terms. Subtract 1 from both sides, since \(\tilde{Y}_t = Y_t/\bar{Y}_t - 1\), and group the constant terms and the \((R_t - \bar{r})\) terms:

\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r}), \qquad \bar{a} \equiv \bar{a}_c + \bar{a}_i + \bar{a}_g + \bar{a}_{nx} - 1 + \bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r}), \qquad \bar{b} \equiv \bar{b}_i + \bar{b}_{nx}. \tag{11}\]

The open-economy IS curve has exactly the form of the closed-economy one, so every tool of the short-run model still works. Only the meaning of the two parameters is richer: \(\bar{b}\) now adds the trade channel to the investment channel, and \(\bar{a}\) now contains a demand shock from abroad.

Why trade reacts like investment. National saving can be used at home or lent abroad: \(S = I + NX\) (Chapter 19). A higher U.S. interest rate makes both uses less attractive at the same time, since borrowing at home costs more while the return abroad stays where it was.

Step 4: the slope. Solve equation (11) for the interest rate: \(R_t - \bar{r} = (\bar{a} - \tilde{Y}_t)/\bar{b}\). With the output gap on the horizontal axis, the IS curve has slope \(-1/\bar{b}\). A larger \(\bar{b}\) makes it flatter. With this notebook’s values, \(\bar{b}_i = 1\) and \(\bar{b}_{nx} = 1\), so \(\bar{b} = 2\): a rise in \(R_t\) from \(\bar{r} = 5\) to 6 percent lowers output by 2 percent, against 1 percent in a closed economy with the same \(\bar{b}_i\) (Fig. 4).

What the model predicts

Change Effect on \(\bar{a}\) or \(\bar{b}\) What moves
domestic real rate \(R_t\) up 1 point none a move along the IS curve: \(\tilde{Y}_t\) falls by \(\bar{b} = \bar{b}_i + \bar{b}_{nx}\), half of it through trade here
foreign real rate \(\bar{R}^w\) up 1 point \(\bar{a}\) rises by \(\bar{b}_{nx}\) the IS curve shifts right
a recession abroad lowers \(\bar{a}_{nx}\) \(\bar{a}\) falls by the same amount the IS curve shifts left
trade more sensitive, \(\bar{b}_{nx}\) up \(\bar{b}\) rises the IS curve gets flatter

In the long run the foreign real rate must equal the world marginal product of capital, \(\bar{R}^w = \bar{r}\), so the foreign term in \(\bar{a}\) vanishes, and \(\bar{a} = 0\) in the long run, as before.

The open economy in the AS/AD model

Assumptions

  1. The open-economy IS curve, equation (11).
  2. The monetary policy rule of Chapter 13: the central bank sets the real interest rate above \(\bar{r}\) when inflation is above its target, \(R_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\).
  3. The Phillips curve with adaptive expectations (Chapter 12), read as an AS curve: \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\).

Solving the model

Step 1: the AD curve. Substitute the policy rule into the IS curve:

\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}). \tag{12}\]

Step 2: where AD meets AS. Put the AS curve into equation (12) and solve for \(\tilde{Y}_t\):

\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t - \bar{\pi}) \;\Longrightarrow\; \tilde{Y}_t(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}) = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi}),\]

\[\tilde{Y}_t = \frac{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi})}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}, \qquad \pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t. \tag{13}\]

Step 3: the dynamics. Call \(x_t \equiv \pi_t - \bar{\pi}\) the inflation gap. Using equation (13) in the AS curve, \(x_t = x_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t = \left(x_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\bar{a}\right)/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\). While \(\bar{a}\) stays constant, this difference equation (Appendix C.10) has the resting point \(x^* = \bar{a}/(\bar{b}\bar{m})\), where output is back at potential, and the gap to it shrinks by the same factor every period:

\[x_t - x^* = \frac{x_{t-1} - x^*}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}.\]

Step 4: a rise in foreign interest rates. In Fig. 5 the foreign real rate rises 2 points above \(\bar{r} = 5\) percent for periods 1 to 9. By equation (11) that is a demand shock \(\bar{a} = \bar{b}_{nx}(\bar{R}^w - \bar{r}) = 1 \times 2 = 2\). With \(\bar{b} = 2\), \(\bar{m} = 1/2\) and \(\bar{\nu} = 1\), we have \(\bar{b}\bar{m} = 1\) and the denominator \(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 2\):

  • period 1: \(\tilde{Y}_1 = (2 - 0)/2 = 1\) percent and \(\pi_1 = 2 + 1 = 3\) percent;
  • periods 2 to 9: the resting point is \(x^* = 2/1 = 2\), so inflation heads for 4 percent, and the remaining gap halves each period (\(\pi_2 = 3.5\), output \(0.5\) percent);
  • period 10: the shock ends, so \(\bar{a} = 0\) and the resting point is back at \(x^* = 0\). With \(\pi_9 \approx 4\), \(\tilde{Y}_{10} = (0 - 1 \times 2)/2 \approx -1\) percent: a recession, after which inflation halves its gap to 2 percent each period.

What the model predicts

  • International transmission of monetary policy. Tighter money abroad weakens the dollar, raises U.S. net exports and works like any positive demand shock at home: a boom, then higher inflation, and a recession when the foreign rate returns to normal. A recession abroad pushes the other way by lowering \(\bar{a}_{nx}\), so the net effect of foreign tightening can have either sign.
  • A larger \(\bar{b}\) makes the AD curve flatter (slope \(-1/(\bar{b}\bar{m})\)). For a given demand shock, output reacts less on impact (the denominator \(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}\) is larger) because the central bank’s interest-rate response is more powerful when it works through trade as well as investment.
Shock in period 1 \(\tilde{Y}_1\) \(\pi_1\) AD curve
\(\bar{R}^w\) up 2 points (Fig. 5), \(\bar{b} = 2\) \(+1\) 3 shifts right by \(\bar{b}_{nx} \times 2 = 2\)
the same shock with \(\bar{b}_{nx} = 0\) 0 2 does not move: no trade channel
a 1-point cut in \(\bar{a}_{nx}\) (recession abroad) \(-0.5\) 1.5 shifts left by 1

The arithmetic of the euro crisis

The euro section of the chapter has no formal model, but three short pieces of arithmetic sit behind its figures.

Definitions

  • Sovereign debt \(D\) is government debt; \(D/Y\) is the debt-GDP ratio, and \(i\) is the nominal interest rate the government pays on it.
  • A bond’s default probability \(p\) is the chance that the government does not repay it.
  • The unit labor cost is the wage cost of one unit of output: the nominal wage \(W\) divided by real output per worker \(Y/L\), \(ULC \equiv W/(Y/L)\).

Solving the model

Step 1: the interest bill. Interest paid each year is \(i \times D\). Divide by \(Y\): interest in percent of GDP is \(i \times (D/Y)\). With debt at 100 percent of GDP, every point on the interest rate costs one point of GDP a year: going from 2 to 6 percent raises the bill from 2 to 6 percent of GDP.

Step 2: why yields converged and then split (Fig. 9). A lender who cares only about the expected return must earn the same on a risky bond as on a safe one, the German bond with rate \(i^{safe}\). If the risky bond pays \(1 + i\) with probability \(1 - p\) and nothing otherwise, then \((1 - p)(1 + i) = 1 + i^{safe}\). Solving for \(i\) and using the approximation of Appendix C.6 for small \(p\) and \(i\):

\[i = \frac{1 + i^{safe}}{1 - p} - 1 \;\approx\; i^{safe} + p. \tag{14}\]

The spread over Germany is roughly the default probability. Before the euro, spreads also contained the expected inflation gap (by the Fisher equation, \(i = R + \pi^e\)); one currency removed that part, so yields converged. After 2008, fear of default opened the spreads again.

Step 3: competitiveness in a currency union (Fig. 13). By the growth rule for a ratio,

\[g_{ULC} = g_W - g_{Y/L}. \tag{15}\]

Inside the euro the nominal exchange rate between Spain and Germany is fixed at one, so their real exchange rate is \(P^{Spain}/P^{Germany}\). If firms set prices as a fixed markup over unit labor cost, equation (5) with \(g_E = 0\) gives \(g_{RER} = g_{ULC}^{Spain} - g_{ULC}^{Germany}\). For example, wages growing 4 percent a year with productivity growing 1 percent in the south, against 1.5 and 1.5 percent in Germany, raise the south’s real exchange rate by about 3 percent a year, or by about a third over a decade, \(1.03^{10} \approx 1.34\).

What the model predicts

  • Self-fulfilling crises. At high debt, a rise in the feared default probability \(p\) raises \(i\) by equation (14), which raises the interest bill, which makes default more likely. Investors’ beliefs can confirm themselves. A central bank that promises to buy the bonds lowers \(p\) and can stop the spiral.
  • No exchange rate to fall back on. A country with its own currency can restore competitiveness by letting \(E\) fall. Inside a monetary union \(g_E = 0\), so the real exchange rate can fall only if wages grow more slowly than productivity at home (equation 15) or faster in Germany, which is slow and painful, and helps explain the high unemployment in southern Europe.

The model in code

We now turn the key results into Python functions. Each function’s description names the equation it computes. The cells after them check the algebra above with numbers.

One baseline for every diagram. The textbook draws its diagrams without numbers. Both model diagrams of this notebook start from one illustrative set of parameters, which the worked numbers above also use:

  • marginal product of capital \(\bar{r} = 5\) percent, as in Chapter 11’s example, and no demand shock at home, \(\bar{a}_c + \bar{a}_i + \bar{a}_g + \bar{a}_{nx} = 1\);
  • interest sensitivities \(\bar{b}_i = 1\) and \(\bar{b}_{nx} = 1\), so the total \(\bar{b} = 2\) is the value of Chapters 11 and 13, split half and half between investment and trade;
  • inflation target \(\bar{\pi} = 2\) percent, policy response \(\bar{m} = 1/2\) and Phillips-curve slope \(\bar{\nu} = 1\), as in Chapter 13;
  • the foreign shock of Fig. 5: the foreign real interest rate is 2 points above \(\bar{r}\), at 7 percent, in periods 1 to 9 and back at \(\bar{r}\) afterwards.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing b_nx=B_NX gives an argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. Names in capital letters, such as R_BAR, are constants that we set once and never change.

R_BAR, B_I, B_NX = 5.0, 1.0, 1.0            # marginal product of capital (%), interest sensitivities
PI_BAR, M_BAR, NU_BAR = 2.0, 0.5, 1.0       # inflation target (%), policy response, Phillips-curve slope
RW_GAP, A_LAST, T_MAX = 2.0, 9, 20          # foreign rate minus r_bar in periods 1-9; periods simulated


def long_run_exchange_rate(P_w, P):
    """Equation (2): the long-run nominal exchange rate E = P_w / P (foreign currency per dollar)."""
    return P_w / P


def real_exchange_rate(E, P, P_w):
    """The real exchange rate E P / P_w: foreign goods needed to buy one U.S. good (equation 3)."""
    return E * P / P_w


def net_exports(R, R_w=R_BAR, a_nx=0.0, b_nx=B_NX):
    """Equation (10): net exports in percent of potential output, NX/Y = a_nx - b_nx (R - R_w)."""
    return a_nx - b_nx * (R - R_w)


def foreign_shock(R_w, b_nx=B_NX, r_bar=R_BAR):
    """The part of a_bar that comes from abroad in equation (11): b_nx (R_w - r_bar)."""
    return b_nx * (R_w - r_bar)
def is_curve(R, a=0.0, b_i=B_I, b_nx=B_NX, r_bar=R_BAR):
    """Equation (11), the open-economy IS curve: Y~ = a - (b_i + b_nx) (R - r_bar), in percent."""
    return a - (b_i + b_nx) * (R - r_bar)


def ad_output(pi, a=0.0, m=M_BAR, b=B_I + B_NX):
    """Equation (12), the AD curve with the open-economy b: Y~ = a - b m (pi - pi_bar)."""
    return a - b * m * (pi - PI_BAR)


def as_inflation(Y, pi_e, nu=NU_BAR):
    """The AS curve of Chapter 13: pi = pi_e + nu Y~, with expected inflation pi_e = last period's inflation."""
    return pi_e + nu * Y


def solve_asad(pi_e, a=0.0, m=M_BAR, b=B_I + B_NX, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Equation (13): the point where the AD and AS curves cross, short-run output and inflation in one period."""
    Y = (a - b * m * (pi_e - PI_BAR)) / (1 + b * m * nu)
    return Y, as_inflation(Y, pi_e, nu)

Let us try the functions on a few textbook cases.

Python note. An f-string such as f"E = {E:.2f}" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text; :.2f means “show two decimals” and :+.1f also shows the sign. Y, pi = solve_asad(...) unpacks the two results of the function into two variables.

E = long_run_exchange_rate(P_w=92.0, P=100.0)       # a chip costs 92 euros in Germany and 100 dollars in the U.S.
print(f"Law of one price: E = {E:.2f} euros per dollar")
print(f"Real exchange rate at that E: {real_exchange_rate(E, 100.0, 92.0):.2f}; at E = 1.00: "
      f"{real_exchange_rate(1.0, 100.0, 92.0):.2f}")
print(f"Net exports when R rises from 5% to 6%: {net_exports(6.0):+.1f}% of potential output")
print(f"IS curve at R = 6%: Y~ = {is_curve(6.0):+.1f}% (without the trade channel: {is_curve(6.0, b_nx=0.0):+.1f}%)")
a = foreign_shock(R_BAR + RW_GAP)
Y, pi = solve_asad(PI_BAR, a)
print(f"Foreign rate 2 points above r_bar: a = {a:.1f}; first period Y~ = {Y:+.2f}%, inflation = {pi:.2f}%")
Law of one price: E = 0.92 euros per dollar
Real exchange rate at that E: 1.00; at E = 1.00: 1.09
Net exports when R rises from 5% to 6%: -1.0% of potential output
IS curve at R = 6%: Y~ = -2.0% (without the trade channel: -1.0%)
Foreign rate 2 points above r_bar: a = 2.0; first period Y~ = +1.00%, inflation = 3.00%

At 0.92 euros per dollar the chip costs the same in both countries, so the real exchange rate is 1. At 1 euro per dollar U.S. chips are about 9 percent too expensive. With the trade channel, a 1-point rise in the interest rate lowers output by 2 percent instead of 1. And a foreign interest rate 2 points above \(\bar{r}\) is a demand shock of \(\bar{a} = 2\): the same shock as Chapter 13’s aggregate demand shock, so the same dynamics follow.

Check 1: money and the long-run exchange rate. Step 2 of the first block says that the elasticity of \(\bar{E}\) with respect to U.S. money is \(-1\). We build both price levels from the quantity theory, \(P = MV/Y\), then double U.S. money and raise it by 1 percent.

def quantity_price(M, V, Y):
    """The long-run price level of the quantity theory: P = M V / Y."""
    return M * V / Y


P_us = quantity_price(M=100.0, V=2.0, Y=2.0)              # 100 dollars per basket
P_de = quantity_price(M=92.0, V=2.0, Y=2.0)               # 92 euros per basket
E_base = long_run_exchange_rate(P_de, P_us)
E_double = long_run_exchange_rate(P_de, quantity_price(M=200.0, V=2.0, Y=2.0))
E_plus1 = long_run_exchange_rate(P_de, quantity_price(M=101.0, V=2.0, Y=2.0))
print(f"Baseline: E = {E_base:.3f} euros per dollar")
print(f"U.S. money doubled: E = {E_double:.3f}  (ratio {E_double / E_base:.3f}, predicted 0.5)")
print(f"U.S. money up 1%:   E changes by {100 * (E_plus1 / E_base - 1):+.3f}%  (predicted about -1%)")
print(f"Real exchange rate in all three cases: {real_exchange_rate(E_base, P_us, P_de):.3f}, "
      f"{real_exchange_rate(E_double, 2 * P_us, P_de):.3f}, {real_exchange_rate(E_plus1, 1.01 * P_us, P_de):.3f}")
Baseline: E = 0.920 euros per dollar
U.S. money doubled: E = 0.460  (ratio 0.500, predicted 0.5)
U.S. money up 1%:   E changes by -0.990%  (predicted about -1%)
Real exchange rate in all three cases: 1.000, 1.000, 1.000

Check 2: PPP in growth rates. We let U.S. prices grow 4 percent a year and Japanese prices 2 percent for 25 years, and recompute the long-run exchange rate from the price levels each year with equation (2). Equation (4) predicts that the dollar falls by about 2 percent a year, and the real exchange rate stays at one.

Python note. A for loop repeats its indented lines, here once for each year 1, 2, …, 25 given by range(1, 26). P = P * 1.04 replaces the old value of P by the new one. np.log is the natural logarithm.

P, P_w = 100.0, 25000.0                 # U.S. dollars and Japanese yen per basket in year 0
E_start = long_run_exchange_rate(P_w, P)
for year in range(1, 26):
    E_last = long_run_exchange_rate(P_w, P)
    P = P * 1.04                        # 4% inflation in the United States
    P_w = P_w * 1.02                    # 2% inflation in Japan
    E_now = long_run_exchange_rate(P_w, P)
    if year in (1, 25):
        growth = 100 * (np.log(E_now) - np.log(E_last))
        print(f"Year {year:2d}: E = {E_now:6.1f} yen per dollar, log growth {growth:+.2f}% "
              f"(equation 4: {2 - 4:+.0f}%), RER = {real_exchange_rate(E_now, P, P_w):.3f}")
print(f"After 25 years E is {E_now / E_start:.3f} times its start; (1.02/1.04)^25 = {(1.02 / 1.04) ** 25:.3f}")
Year  1: E =  245.2 yen per dollar, log growth -1.94% (equation 4: -2%), RER = 1.000
Year 25: E =  153.9 yen per dollar, log growth -1.94% (equation 4: -2%), RER = 1.000
After 25 years E is 0.615 times its start; (1.02/1.04)^25 = 0.615

The log growth rate is \(-1.94\) percent rather than exactly \(-2\): equation (4) is the approximation \(\ln(1.02/1.04) \approx 0.02 - 0.04\).

Check 3: the Balassa-Samuelson effect. We compute the real exchange rate step by step, from wages to the prices of the two goods to the price level, and compare it with the closed form of equation (6). Home’s traded-goods productivity doubles; everything else stays at one, and \(\theta = 1/2\).

def bs_price_level(P_T, A_T, A_N, theta=0.5):
    """Price level P = P_T^theta P_N^(1-theta), with P_N from equal wages: P_T A_T = P_N A_N."""
    wage = P_T * A_T                        # value of a worker's output in the traded sector
    P_N = wage / A_N                        # the same wage paid in the nontraded sector
    return P_T ** theta * P_N ** (1 - theta)


E_now, P_T_home = 0.92, 100.0
P_T_abroad = E_now * P_T_home               # the law of one price for traded goods
step_by_step = real_exchange_rate(E_now, bs_price_level(P_T_home, A_T=2.0, A_N=1.0),
                                  bs_price_level(P_T_abroad, A_T=1.0, A_N=1.0))
closed_form = ((2.0 / 1.0) / (1.0 / 1.0)) ** (1 - 0.5)
print(f"RER step by step: {step_by_step:.4f}   equation (6): {closed_form:.4f}")
print(f"Productivity gap of 3 points a year for 24 years, theta = 1/2: RER x {1.015 ** 24:.2f}")
RER step by step: 1.4142   equation (6): 1.4142
Productivity gap of 3 points a year for 24 years, theta = 1/2: RER x 1.43

Check 4: uncovered interest parity. Start with equal interest rates, 5 percent at home and abroad, and an anchor of 0.92 euros per dollar. Raise the U.S. rate to 6 percent. Equation (7) gives the exact jump, equation (8) the approximation: about 1 percent if the gap lasts one year, about 5 percent if it lasts five, the slope that Fig. 7 uses.

def uip_exchange_rate(E_anchor, i, i_w, years=1):
    """Today's exchange rate from UIP, equation (7) applied `years` times: E = E_anchor ((1 + i) / (1 + i_w))^years."""
    return E_anchor * ((1 + i / 100) / (1 + i_w / 100)) ** years


for years in (1, 5):
    E_now = uip_exchange_rate(0.92, i=6.0, i_w=5.0, years=years)
    jump = 100 * (E_now / 0.92 - 1)
    print(f"Gap lasting {years} year(s): E = {E_now:.4f}, a jump of {jump:+.2f}% (equation 8: {years * 1.0:+.1f}%)")
E_now = uip_exchange_rate(0.92, i=6.0, i_w=5.0)
print(f"Return in dollars: at home {1.06:.4f}; abroad {E_now * 1.05 / 0.92:.4f}  (equal, as UIP requires)")
Gap lasting 1 year(s): E = 0.9288, a jump of +0.95% (equation 8: +1.0%)
Gap lasting 5 year(s): E = 0.9647, a jump of +4.85% (equation 8: +5.0%)
Return in dollars: at home 1.0600; abroad 1.0600  (equal, as UIP requires)

Check 5: a peg. With a credible peg, equation (7) gives \(i = i^w\), equation (9). If markets expect a 10 percent devaluation, the same equation tells us the interest rate needed to defend the peg.

def defend_peg_rate(i_w, expected_fall):
    """Interest rate (%) that keeps UIP, equation (7), when E is fixed today and expected to fall by `expected_fall` %."""
    E_ratio = 1 / (1 - expected_fall / 100)              # E_fix / E_expected
    return 100 * ((1 + i_w / 100) * E_ratio - 1)


print(f"Credible peg, no fall expected: i = {defend_peg_rate(5.0, 0.0):.2f}%  (equation 9: i = i_w = 5%)")
print(f"Devaluation of 10% expected:    i = {defend_peg_rate(5.0, 10.0):.2f}%  (rough rule: 5 + 10 = 15%)")
Credible peg, no fall expected: i = 5.00%  (equation 9: i = i_w = 5%)
Devaluation of 10% expected:    i = 16.67%  (rough rule: 5 + 10 = 15%)

The rough rule $i i^w + $ expected depreciation understates the exact answer here, because a 10 percent fall is not a small change, and the approximations of Appendix C.6 work best for small ones.

Check 6: the IS curve from its pieces. We add up the spending shares one by one, with \(\bar{a}_c = 60\), \(\bar{a}_i = 20\), \(\bar{a}_g = 20\) and \(\bar{a}_{nx} = 0\) percent of potential output, and compare \(Y/\bar{Y} - 1\) with equation (11), at a U.S. rate of 6 percent and a foreign rate of 7 percent.

R, R_w = 6.0, 7.0
consumption = 60.0
investment = 20.0 - B_I * (R - R_BAR)
government = 20.0
trade = net_exports(R, R_w=R_w)                          # equation (10)
by_pieces = consumption + investment + government + trade - 100
print(f"Shares: C {consumption:.0f} + I {investment:.0f} + G {government:.0f} + NX {trade:+.0f} - 100 = {by_pieces:+.1f}%")
print(f"Equation (11): Y~ = {is_curve(R, a=foreign_shock(R_w)):+.1f}%")
print(f"Slope check: a 1-point rise in R moves Y~ by {is_curve(R + 1) - is_curve(R):+.1f} (open) "
      f"and {is_curve(R + 1, b_nx=0.0) - is_curve(R, b_nx=0.0):+.1f} (closed)")
Shares: C 60 + I 19 + G 20 + NX +1 - 100 = +0.0%
Equation (11): Y~ = +0.0%
Slope check: a 1-point rise in R moves Y~ by -2.0 (open) and -1.0 (closed)

Check 7: the dynamics of a foreign shock. Step 3 of the AS/AD block says that, while the shock lasts, the inflation gap to its resting point \(x^* = \bar{a}/(\bar{b}\bar{m}) = 2\) halves each period. We follow the economy with solve_asad and compare.

a, bm = foreign_shock(R_BAR + RW_GAP), (B_I + B_NX) * M_BAR
x_star = a / bm                                          # resting point of the inflation gap
pi_e = PI_BAR
for t in range(1, 11):
    if t <= A_LAST:
        Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, a)
    else:
        Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, 0.0)                    # the shock ends after period 9
    formula = x_star - x_star / (1 + bm * NU_BAR) ** t   # x_t from step 3, valid while the shock lasts
    if t in (1, 2, 9):
        print(f"Period {t:2d}: Y~ = {Y:+.3f}%, pi = {pi:.3f}%   (step 3: pi = {PI_BAR + formula:.3f}%)")
    pi_e = pi
print(f"Period 10: Y~ = {Y:+.3f}%, pi = {pi:.3f}%   (the shock has ended: a recession)")
print(f"On the AD curve? {ad_output(pi, 0.0):+.3f} = {Y:+.3f}")
Period  1: Y~ = +1.000%, pi = 3.000%   (step 3: pi = 3.000%)
Period  2: Y~ = +0.500%, pi = 3.500%   (step 3: pi = 3.500%)
Period  9: Y~ = +0.004%, pi = 3.996%   (step 3: pi = 3.996%)
Period 10: Y~ = -0.998%, pi = 2.998%   (the shock has ended: a recession)
On the AD curve? -0.998 = -0.998

The simulation and the formula agree while the shock lasts. In period 10 the formula no longer applies, because the shock has ended, and output drops to about \(-1\) percent, as computed in step 4.

One loop for the dynamics

Fig. 5 follows the economy period by period. Each period, firms expect last period’s inflation, and the economy jumps to the point where that period’s AD and AS curves cross. simulate repeats this step; shock_list builds the list of demand shocks, one value per period.

Python note. values.append(x) adds x at the end of the list values, and for t in range(1, 21) repeats the indented lines for t = 1, 2, …, 20. dict(period=0, Y=0.0) is a dictionary, a set of named values, and rows[-1]["pi"] is the value named "pi" in the last element of the list. pd.DataFrame(rows) turns a list of dictionaries into a table, one row per dictionary.

def shock_list(size, last=A_LAST):
    """A demand shock of the given size in periods 1, ..., last and zero afterwards, for T_MAX periods."""
    values = []
    for t in range(1, T_MAX + 1):
        if t <= last:
            values.append(size)
        else:
            values.append(0.0)
    return values


def simulate(a_list, m=M_BAR, b=B_I + B_NX, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Solve the AS/AD model period by period; period 0 is the steady state (Y~ = 0, pi = pi_bar)."""
    rows = [dict(period=0, a=0.0, pi_e=PI_BAR, Y=0.0, pi=PI_BAR)]
    for t in range(1, len(a_list) + 1):
        pi_e = rows[-1]["pi"]                   # adaptive expectations: last period's inflation
        Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, a_list[t - 1], m, b, nu)
        rows.append(dict(period=t, a=a_list[t - 1], pi_e=pi_e, Y=Y, pi=pi))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


simulate(shock_list(2.0)).loc[[0, 1, 2, 8, 9, 10, 11]].round(3)
period a pi_e Y pi
0 0 0.0 2.000 0.000 2.000
1 1 2.0 2.000 1.000 3.000
2 2 2.0 3.000 0.500 3.500
8 8 2.0 3.984 0.008 3.992
9 9 2.0 3.992 0.004 3.996
10 10 0.0 3.996 -0.998 2.998
11 11 0.0 2.998 -0.499 2.499

Inflation rises from 2 to 3 percent in period 1 and climbs toward 4 percent while the shock lasts. When the shock ends in period 10, output falls below potential and inflation starts back down to 2 percent.

Drawing tools

Both model diagrams use the same few drawing steps, so we write them once:

  • add_curve draws a curve and writes its name at its last point inside the axes, as the textbook does;
  • add_point marks a point with a dot, a letter and dashed guides to the axes;
  • add_arrow draws an arrow between two points.

Python note. (x >= 0) & (y <= 8) is true where both conditions hold, x[inside] keeps the values where inside is true, and [-1] takes the last of them. add_annotation with axref="x" and ayref="y" draws an arrow from (ax, ay) to (x, y), both in axis units. Labels such as "AS<sub>8</sub>" use HTML to write AS₈.

def add_curve(fig, x, y, label, color, x_range, y_range, dash="solid"):
    """Draw one curve and write its label at its last point inside the axes (no label if label is "")."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=y, mode="lines", name=label, showlegend=False,
                             line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash=dash)))
    inside = (x >= x_range[0]) & (x <= x_range[1]) & (y >= y_range[0]) & (y <= y_range[1])
    if inside.any() and label != "":
        fig.add_annotation(x=x[inside][-1], y=y[inside][-1], text=label, showarrow=False,
                           xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", font=dict(color=color, size=14))


def add_point(fig, x, y, label, x0, y0, guides=True):
    """Mark the point (x, y) with a dot and a label; with guides, dashed lines to the axes at x0 and y0."""
    if guides:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[x0, x, x], y=[y, y, y0], mode="lines", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                                 line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[x], y=[y], mode="markers+text", text=[label], textposition="top right",
                             name=label, showlegend=False, textfont=dict(size=16), marker=dict(color="black", size=10)))


def add_arrow(fig, x0, y0, x1, y1, color="black"):
    """Draw an arrow from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1) in axis units; nothing if the two points almost coincide."""
    if abs(x1 - x0) + abs(y1 - y0) > 0.15:
        fig.add_annotation(x=x1, y=y1, ax=x0, ay=y0, xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y", text="",
                           showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor=color)

Tools for comparing countries

The textbook’s data figures show a few countries. Every one of them can show many more: the data files of this chapter hold the same series for up to 200 economies, from the World Bank, the IMF, the OECD, the Federal Reserve and the Penn World Table. The file countries.csv lists the economies with their World Bank region and income group, and says which are OECD members and since when each euro member uses the euro.

country_info = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")
country_info[country_info.country.isin(["Japan", "Germany", "Mexico", "Euro area"])]
iso3 country region income oecd euro_since
53 DEU Germany Europe & Central Asia High income True 1999.0
61 EMU Euro area Euro area High income False NaN
102 JPN Japan East Asia & Pacific High income True NaN
129 MEX Mexico Latin America & Caribbean Upper middle income True NaN

Three small tools are shared by the data figures:

  • group_colors gives every country a fixed color, so a line keeps its color when you add or remove others. The textbook’s countries keep the textbook’s colors, and the countries of one menu group (the G7, a region, …) never share a color, as far as Plotly’s 44 dark enough colors allow;
  • ratio_ticks chooses round tick values for a ratio-scale axis that spans less than a factor of 10 (Plotly’s own ticks crowd there; over wider spans we let Plotly choose);
  • missing_note adds a note to a title when a chosen country has no data;
  • high_low names the countries with the highest and the lowest value, for the titles;
  • book_order puts the textbook’s countries first in a bar chart.

Python note. px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 and .Alphabet are lists of colors that Plotly provides; we drop the pale ones. In group_colors, for each country, score gives every color a cost: 1 for each country that already uses it, 10 for each one in a large group (Europe has more countries than there are colors) and 100 for each one in a group small enough to avoid any clash. a if test else b gives a when the test is True. min(PALETTE, key=score.get) picks the color with the lowest cost (the first one on ties). When no color is free, PALETTE[::-1] (the list in reverse order) makes the search start from the end of the list, so that the leftovers take the last, rarely used colors.

LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]     # too pale on a white background
PALETTE = []
for color in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 + px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:   # 24 + 26 colors, 44 of them kept
    if color not in LIGHT and color != "#2E91E5":
        PALETTE.append(color)
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")                       # Dark24's medium blue goes last: it is close to the book's navy
def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """A color for each country that no other country in its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    groups: the lists of countries shown together (the menu views); fixed: the textbook countries' colors."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in sorted(names):
        if name in colors:
            continue
        score = {}                                  # the cost of each color: lower is better
        for color in PALETTE:
            score[color] = list(colors.values()).count(color)            # 1 per country using it anywhere
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                weight = 100 if len(group) <= len(PALETTE) else 10      # a clash in a small group costs most
                for other in group:
                    if colors.get(other) in score:
                        score[colors[other]] += weight
        best = min(PALETTE, key=score.get)                              # the cheapest color
        if score[best] >= 10:                       # no free color: the least used one, searching from the end
            best = min(PALETTE[::-1], key=score.get)
        colors[name] = best
    return colors
def ratio_ticks(low, high):
    """Round tick values between low and high for a ratio-scale axis; None (Plotly's ticks) beyond a factor of 10."""
    if high / low >= 10:
        return None
    ticks = []
    for power in range(-3, 6):
        for step in [1, 1.2, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]:
            if low <= step * 10 ** power <= high:
                ticks.append(round(step * 10 ** power, 6))
    return ticks

Python note. ", ".join(missing) glues a list of texts into one text, with ", " between them. In f"{value:{fmt}}" the format itself is a variable: fmt=".0f" shows no decimals, ".1f" one. In a Plotly title, <br> starts a new line and <sup>...</sup> writes smaller text.

def missing_note(wanted, found):
    """A second, smaller title line naming the chosen countries that have no data ('' if all have data)."""
    missing = []
    for name in wanted:
        if name not in set(found):
            missing.append(name)
    if len(missing) == 0:
        return ""
    if len(missing) > 3:
        return f"<br><sup>no data for {len(missing)} of the chosen countries</sup>"
    return "<br><sup>no data: " + ", ".join(missing) + "</sup>"
def high_low(values, fmt=".0f"):
    """'A 12, B 3': the countries with the highest and the lowest value (one name only for one country)."""
    text = f"{values.idxmax()} {values.max():{fmt}}"
    if len(values) > 1:
        text = text + f", {values.idxmin()} {values.min():{fmt}}"
    return text


def book_order(countries, book):
    """The textbook's countries in the textbook's order, then the others alphabetically (for bar charts)."""
    order = []
    for name in book:
        if name in countries:
            order.append(name)
    for name in sorted(countries):
        if name not in order:
            order.append(name)
    return order


print(ratio_ticks(67, 142), ratio_ticks(1, 50), missing_note(("Japan", "Kosovo"), ["Japan"]))
print(high_low(pd.Series({"Japan": 2.4, "Switzerland": 2.2, "United States": 4.0}), ".1f"))
[70, 80, 90, 100, 120.0] None <br><sup>no data: Kosovo</sup>
United States 4.0, Switzerland 2.2

In Colab each figure gets a list of countries: click a name to choose it, and hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) while you click to choose several. On the website, click a country in the legend, or pick a group of countries in the menu.

Exchange rates in the long run

We start with the data: how the dollar has moved against the yen and the euro, and whether the gap in inflation between two countries explains the move, as the law of one price predicts.

Fig. 1: The U.S. exchange rate versus the yen and the euro

Goal. See how the price of a dollar has moved since the end of fixed exchange rates in 1971.

The exchange rate here is the price of a dollar in foreign currency: how many yen, or how many euros, one dollar buys. A fall is a depreciation of the dollar, a rise an appreciation. The two series have very different units (hundreds of yen, about one euro), so the textbook draws them on two vertical scales.

Python note. parse_dates=["date"] tells read_csv that the column date holds dates, so Plotly draws a proper time axis. .tail() shows the last five rows. The euro only exists since 1999, so the column eur_per_usd is empty (NaN, “not a number”) before that.

fx = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig20-1.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
fx.tail()

Each row is a month: yen_per_usd is the average number of yen per dollar, and eur_per_usd the number of euros per dollar (the Federal Reserve publishes dollars per euro; the data file turns it around so that both lines are the price of a dollar).

Python note. px.line draws the yen line. add_scatter(..., yaxis="y2") adds the euro line on a second vertical axis, which yaxis2=dict(overlaying="y", side="right") places on the right. hovermode="x unified" shows both values of the month you point at in one box.

Sources. Data: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, H.10 Foreign Exchange Rates, via FRED: Japanese yen to one U.S. dollar (EXJPUS) and U.S. dollars to one euro (EXUSEU) (inverted to euros per dollar), monthly. Prepared file: data/ch20/fig20-1.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 20.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • From 1971 to 1995 the dollar lost three quarters of its value against the yen: from 358 yen in January 1971 to 84 in April 1995.
  • Against the euro the dollar first appreciated, to 1.17 euros in October 2000, then depreciated to 0.63 in July 2008, and has been between about 0.8 and 1.0 euros in most years since 2015.
  • The newest data go beyond the textbook: in 2024–2026 the dollar bought 143 to 162 yen. The 162 yen of July 2026 are the most since 1986.

Key numbers: the dates in the text

Python note. fx.set_index("date") uses the dates as row labels, and .loc[...] picks rows by label. pd.to_datetime([...]) turns a list of texts into dates, so that they match the row labels.

Other currencies against the dollar

The Federal Reserve publishes the same monthly rates for 20 other currencies, and until 2001 for the German mark, the French franc and the Italian lira, which the euro replaced. Their units differ enormously (in September 2026 a dollar bought 1,359 won but 0.82 Swiss francs), so to compare them we turn each one into an index: the price of a dollar divided by its average in a base year, times 100. An index of 120 means a dollar buys 20 percent more of that currency than in the base year: the dollar has appreciated by 20 percent.

Python note. .str[:4] keeps the first four characters of each text (the year of "1999-01"), and .astype(int) turns them into numbers. Adding text columns with + glues the texts together.

fx_all = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fx_monthly.csv")
fx_all["year"] = fx_all.date.str[:4].astype(int)
fx_all["label"] = fx_all.country + " (" + fx_all.currency + ")"
fx_all.tail(3)
iso3 country currency date per_usd year label
14129 ZAF South Africa rand 2026-07 16.466 2026 South Africa (rand)
14130 ZAF South Africa rand 2026-08 16.165 2026 South Africa (rand)
14131 ZAF South Africa rand 2026-09 16.222 2026 South Africa (rand)

Python note. isin(countries) is true in the rows whose country is in the list. groupby("country").mean() averages the base-year months of each country, and .map(level) looks up that average for every row. A currency with no data in the base year gets NaN, and dropna removes it; missing_note then names it in the title. idxmax() gives the label of the largest value. log_y=True draws a ratio scale.

FX_COLORS = group_colors(fx_all.label.unique(), [list(fx_all.label.unique())],      # all in one legend
                         {"Japan (yen)": BLUE, "Euro area (euro)": TEAL})


def dollar_index(countries=("Japan", "Euro area"), base=1999, scale="linear"):
    """Fig. 20.1 for any currency: units of the currency per dollar, index = 100 in the base year."""
    picked = fx_all[fx_all.country.isin(countries)].copy()
    level = picked[picked.year == base].groupby("country").per_usd.mean()     # average of the base year
    picked["index"] = (100 * picked.per_usd / picked.country.map(level)).round(1)
    picked = picked.dropna(subset=["index"])
    latest = picked.groupby("country")["index"].last()                        # each currency's last month
    title = f"No data in {base} for these currencies"
    if len(latest) > 0:
        title = f"Price of a dollar ({base} = 100), latest: " + high_low(latest)
    fig = px.line(picked, x="date", y="index", color="label", hover_name="label", color_discrete_map=FX_COLORS,
                  log_y=(scale == "ratio"), title=title + missing_note(countries, level.index),
                  labels={"date": "Year", "index": f"Price of a dollar ({base} = 100)"})
    fig.add_hline(y=100, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
    if scale == "ratio" and len(picked) > 0:
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=ratio_ticks(picked["index"].min(), picked["index"].max()))
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="", xaxis_range=["1965-01-01", "2027-06-01"])   # no tick label in the corner
    return fig
interact(dollar_index,
         countries=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(fx_all.country.unique()), value=("Japan", "Euro area"), rows=8,
                                  description="currencies", style=WIDE),
         base=Dropdown(options=[1971, 1985, 1999, 2010, 2020], value=1999, description="base year", style=WIDE),

Fig. 2: Inflation in the United States and Japan

Goal. Check the law of one price’s prediction: if the dollar depreciated against the yen for decades, U.S. inflation must have been higher than Japan’s.

Write equation (2) in growth rates, as in equation (4) of the Model overview. With \(E\) = yen per dollar, \(P^w\) the Japanese and \(P\) the U.S. price level,

\[\frac{\Delta \bar{E}}{\bar{E}} \approx \pi^{w} - \pi,\]

so the dollar loses value against the yen by roughly the gap between U.S. and Japanese inflation.

INFLATION_GROUPS = country_groups(inflation_all.country.unique(), ["United States", "Japan"],
                                  "Textbook: U.S. and Japan")                  # the website menu

def inflation_chart(countries=("United States", "Japan")):
    """Fig. 20.2 for any countries: consumer-price inflation, percent per year."""
    picked = inflation_all[inflation_all.country.isin(countries)]
    means = picked[(picked.year >= 1971) & (picked.year <= 2024)].groupby("country").inflation.mean()
    title = "No inflation data for these countries"
    if len(means) > 0:
        title = "Mean inflation 1971–2024 (%): " + high_low(means, ".1f")
    top = 25.0
    if len(picked) > 0:
        top = min(max(25.0, 1.05 * picked.inflation.max()), 100.0)
    if len(picked) > 0 and picked.inflation.max() > 100:
        title = title + "; axis cut at 100"
    fig = px.line(picked, x="year", y="inflation", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=INFLATION_COLORS, title=title + missing_note(countries, means.index),
                  labels={"year": "Year", "inflation": "Inflation (percent per year)"})
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    bottom = min(-3.0, picked.inflation.min() - 1) if len(picked) > 0 else -3.0
    fig.update_layout(yaxis_range=[bottom, top], xaxis_range=[1955, 2026], legend_title_text="")   # 1960 off the corner
    return fig

Prepared files: data/ch20/inflation_wdi.csv and data/ch20/countries.csv, checked against data/ch20/fig20-2.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 20.2 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

Pick a group in the menu, then click a country in the legend to hide or show it.

What to notice.

  • Japan’s inflation jumped to 23 percent in 1974, after the first oil shock; U.S. inflation peaked at 13.5 percent in 1980.
  • From the late 1990s Japan had deflation in many years (falling prices), while U.S. inflation stayed positive except in 2009.
  • Over 1971–2024 U.S. inflation averaged 4.0 percent a year and Japan’s 2.4 percent. Add Switzerland (2.2 percent) and Germany (2.7 percent): the countries with the lowest inflation are those whose currencies gained the most against the dollar in Fig. 1.
  • Look at your data: add Argentina and you get only seven points, 2018–2024. Argentina’s official consumer price index was discredited in 2007–2015 and restarted in 2016–2017, and the World Bank’s series begins after that, so even the hyperinflation of 1989–1990 is missing from this file.

Key numbers: average inflation

for first, last in [(1971, 1995), (1996, 2024), (1971, 2024)]:
    span = inflation[(inflation.year >= first) & (inflation.year <= last)]
    us, jp = span.inflation_us.mean(), span.inflation_jpn.mean()
    print(f"{first}–{last}: United States {us:.2f}%, Japan {jp:.2f}%, gap {us - jp:.2f} points a year")
1971–1995: United States 5.67%, Japan 4.74%, gap 0.93 points a year
1996–2024: United States 2.53%, Japan 0.43%, gap 2.10 points a year
1971–2024: United States 3.98%, Japan 2.43%, gap 1.56 points a year

Between 1971 and 1995 U.S. inflation was higher by only about 1 point a year, as the textbook says. Fig. 3 shows why that small gap cannot explain the dollar’s fall from 358 to 84 yen.

Table 20.1: the Big Mac index

The Economist compares the price of a Big Mac around the world. If the law of one price held for burgers, a Big Mac would cost the same number of dollars everywhere. The data file big_mac.csv holds every release of the index since 2000, made by data/ch20/build_data.py from The Economist’s open data.

big_mac = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "big_mac.csv")
big_mac.head()
release iso3 country currency local_price ex_rate dollar_price gdp_pc_2023
0 2000-04-01 ARG Argentina ARS 2.50 1.00 2.50 27285.0
1 2000-04-01 AUS Australia AUD 2.59 1.68 1.54 64333.0
2 2000-04-01 BRA Brazil BRL 2.95 1.79 1.65 18713.0
3 2000-04-01 CAN Canada CAD 2.85 1.47 1.94 55101.0
4 2000-04-01 CHE Switzerland CHF 5.90 1.70 3.47 89957.0

Each row is one economy in one release: the local price, the market exchange rate (local currency per dollar) and the dollar price, local price / exchange rate. gdp_pc_2023 is GDP per person from the Penn World Table, which we use in Fig. 3.

Python note. set_index("country") uses the country names as row labels, and .loc[BOOK_ROWS] picks the rows in the order of the list. A new column is created simply by assigning to it: table["vs_US_percent"] = ....

BOOK_ROWS = ["United States", "Norway", "Euro area", "Mexico", "China", "Japan", "South Africa", "India"]


def big_mac_table(release="2022-07-01"):
    """Table 20.1: Big Mac prices in local currency and in dollars, for one release of the index."""
    table = big_mac[big_mac.release == release].set_index("country").loc[BOOK_ROWS]
    us_price = table.loc["United States", "dollar_price"]
    table["vs_US_percent"] = 100 * (table.dollar_price / us_price - 1)      # dearer (+) or cheaper (-) than in the U.S.
    return table[["local_price", "currency", "ex_rate", "dollar_price", "vs_US_percent"]].round(2)

table["textbook"] = pd.Series({"United States": 5.15, "Norway": 6.26, "Euro area": 4.74, "Mexico": 3.43,

  • By the burger standard, Norway’s krone was overvalued (21.6 percent dearer than in the U.S.) and China’s yuan undervalued (30.9 percent cheaper).
