# Your turn: try it here

Concluding remarks

  • The nominal exchange rate is the price of a currency; the real exchange rate \(EP/P^w\) is the price of goods. In the long run the law of one price, equation (1), sets the real exchange rate to 1, equation (3), and ties the nominal rate to relative price levels, equation (2). In growth rates, equation (4), more inflation means a weaker currency.
  • The law of one price holds only loosely. Japan’s real exchange rate rose 2.5-fold until 1995, and Big Macs cost more in rich countries: nontraded goods get dearer as wages rise (the Balassa-Samuelson effect, equation 6).
  • In the short run, prices are sticky and the exchange rate moves with interest rates (uncovered interest parity, equations 7 and 8). Net exports then react to the interest rate like investment, equation (10), which makes the IS curve flatter, equation (11), and a rise in foreign interest rates is a positive demand shock at home that ends in a recession when it is reversed (the AS/AD solution, equations 12 and 13).
  • The policy trilemma: an open economy can have at most two of a stable exchange rate, monetary autonomy and free capital flows; a credible peg with free flows forces \(i = i^w\), equation (9). Gold, Bretton Woods, currency boards, capital controls and the euro are different choices of two, and the crises in Mexico, Asia, Argentina and the euro area show what happens when a choice breaks down: default risk opens bond spreads, equation (14), and a currency union can regain competitiveness only through unit labor costs, equation (15).
  • The next chapter, Parting Thoughts, looks back at the whole book and at the open questions of macroeconomics.

Practice problems

These problems use the chapter’s tools in three ways: conceptual problems apply its equations to real episodes, data-based problems send you back to its data files, and modeling problems answer policy questions with its interactive models. Each one is marked Basic, Intermediate or Challenge; try it on your own first, and open the Hint and the Solution only after that. The sliders in the answer cells run in Colab (open this notebook with the badge at the top); on the website, use the website version of each figure above.

Conceptual problems

Problem 1 (Basic): Croatia swaps the kuna for the euro. On 1 January 2023 Croatia replaced its currency, the kuna, with the euro, at a conversion rate fixed by the Council of the European Union: 7.53450 kuna per euro. In the IMF data of Fig. 8 (fx_crises.csv), one dollar bought 7.06403 kuna and 0.937559 euros at the end of 2022.

  1. Suppose a cup of coffee cost 11.30 kuna in December 2022 (an illustrative price). What did it cost in euros on 1 January 2023?

  2. Write the price of a dollar in Croatia in euros instead of kuna. How does it compare with the euro area’s rate?

  3. Use the definition of the real exchange rate, \(EP/P^w\) (step 3 of the first block of the Model overview), to show that the switch changed neither the real exchange rate between the United States and Croatia nor any other real variable.

  4. If nothing real changed on 1 January 2023, what did Croatia give up by adopting the euro? Use equation (9).

Hint

The switch divides every amount written in kuna by the same number, 7.53450: prices, wages, and the price of a dollar. What happens to a ratio when its top and its bottom are divided by the same number? For (d), ask who sets Croatia’s interest rate after the switch.

Your answer:

Solution

(a) \(11.30 / 7.53450 = 1.4998\), so the coffee costs 1.50 euros.

(b) A dollar bought 7.06403 kuna, so it buys \(7.06403 / 7.53450 = 0.93756\) euros: exactly the euro area’s rate of 0.937559 euros per dollar, up to rounding. From that day Croatia simply shares the euro area’s exchange rate.

(c) Take the United States as home, so \(E\) is Croatian money per dollar, \(P\) the U.S. price level in dollars and \(P^w\) the Croatian price level in Croatian money. Call the conversion rate \(c = 7.53450\). The switch divides both \(E\) and \(P^w\) by \(c\), and leaves \(P\) alone:

\[RER_{\text{after}} = \frac{(E/c)\,P}{P^w/c} = \frac{EP}{P^w} = RER_{\text{before}}.\]

A cup of coffee in Zagreb costs as many U.S. goods as it did the day before. The same holds for every other real variable, because each one is a ratio of two amounts in the same money (a real wage \(W/P\), the real value of savings, real GDP): the \(c\) cancels. This is the classical dichotomy of the Model overview: the level of the nominal exchange rate has no meaning of its own.

(d) Inside the euro area Croatia’s exchange rate with the other members is fixed for good and money flows freely, so by equation (9) its interest rate is the ECB’s, \(i = i^w\). Croatia gave up its own monetary policy, and with it the option to devalue against its main trading partners: the tool that Greece, Spain and Portugal lacked after 2010 (equation (15) and Fig. 13). In practice the kuna was already tied closely to the euro: in our data it stayed between 7.41 and 7.65 kuna per euro at the end of every year from 2011 to 2022. The big change in policy had happened before the switch.

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Hong Kong’s peg meets the Fed. Hong Kong runs a currency board: its Monetary Authority promises to trade Hong Kong dollars for U.S. dollars at 7.75 and at 7.85 Hong Kong dollars per U.S. dollar, the two edges of a narrow band. In our data (fx_monthly.csv, from the Federal Reserve’s H.10 release), the monthly average has stayed between 7.7497 and 7.8498 since June 2005. Between March 2022 and July 2023 the Federal Reserve raised its target range for the federal funds rate from 0–0.25 percent to 5.25–5.50 percent, and on 27 July 2023 the Hong Kong Monetary Authority set its Base Rate at 5.75 percent, by a formula that puts it at least 0.5 point above the lower end of the Fed’s range. Yet in 2022 Hong Kong’s real GDP fell by 3.7 percent, while U.S. real GDP grew by 2.4 percent.

  1. Which equation of the Model overview explains why Hong Kong’s interest rates rose with the Fed’s, even though its economy shrank? Which goal of the policy trilemma did Hong Kong give up?

  2. Suppose investors suddenly expect the Hong Kong dollar to be devalued by 5 percent within a year, while the one-year U.S. rate is 5.25 percent. What one-year Hong Kong rate keeps them willing to hold Hong Kong dollars? What if they expect a devaluation of 20 percent? Compare both answers with the rough rule \(i \approx i^w +\) expected depreciation.

  3. A critic says Hong Kong should let its currency float, so that it can cut interest rates in a recession. Name one gain and one cost of that change. Then explain when the third option of the trilemma, capital controls, would be costly.

Hint

For (a), a credible peg means \(E_t = E^e_{t+1}\); put that into equation (7). For (b), solve equation (7) for \(i_t\) with \(E_{fix}/E^e_{t+1} = 1/(1 - 0.05)\), or use the function defend_peg_rate of Check 5. For (c), look at the table of regimes at the end of the policy-trilemma block.

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution

(a) Equation (9), \(i_t = i^w\). When investors believe the peg, they expect no change in the exchange rate, so the ratio \(E_t/E^e_{t+1}\) in equation (7) is one, and Hong Kong’s interest rate must equal the U.S. rate. If it stayed lower, money would flow out of Hong Kong dollars into U.S. dollars until the peg broke. That is why the Base Rate follows the Fed by formula, whatever Hong Kong’s own economy needs. Hong Kong gave up monetary autonomy; it keeps a stable exchange rate and free financial flows, the currency-board side of the triangle in Fig. 7.

(b) Solve equation (7) for the interest rate, with \(E_{fix}/E^e_{t+1} = 1/(1 - d)\) for an expected devaluation \(d\):

\[1 + i = \frac{1 + i^w}{1 - d} = \frac{1.0525}{0.95} = 1.1079, \qquad\text{so}\qquad i = 10.79 \text{ percent},\]

against \(5.25 + 5 = 10.25\) percent by the rough rule. With \(d = 0.20\), \(1 + i = 1.0525/0.80 = 1.3156\), so \(i = 31.56\) percent, against 25.25 percent by the rough rule. The bigger the fear, the more the rough rule understates the rate needed, because the approximation of Appendix C.6 only works for small changes. A rate above 30 percent in a recession is the kind of cost that makes governments abandon a peg (Fig. 8).

for fall in [5.0, 20.0]:
    exact = defend_peg_rate(5.25, fall)                    # equation (7) solved for i
    print(f"Expected devaluation {fall:.0f}%: i = {exact:.2f}% (rough rule: {5.25 + fall:.2f}%)")

(c) Gain: with a floating rate Hong Kong could have kept its rates low in 2022, when its GDP fell. By equation (8) its currency would then have depreciated against the U.S. dollar, which also makes its exports cheaper. Cost: the exchange rate would move every day. Among the floating currencies of Fig. 6, the typical yearly change is 8 to 13 percent, a new risk for every firm and bank that trades or borrows in U.S. dollars, and a peg that has held near 7.8 since 17 October 1983 (HKMA, Linked Exchange Rate System; in our data, between 7.7245 and 7.852 from November 1983, its first full month) would be gone. Capital controls would let Hong Kong keep both its own interest rate and the peg, but only by rationing who may exchange currency. That is costly for any economy that lives from lending, borrowing and trading assets with the rest of the world, because the controls block exactly those flows.

Problem 3 (Challenge): Catching up inside the euro. A hypothetical country, Home, joins the euro area. Output per worker in Home’s traded sector grows 5 percent a year and in its nontraded sector 1 percent; in the rest of the euro area the two grow 2 and 1 percent. Both use the weight \(\theta = 1/2\) on traded goods in the price level, and the ECB keeps inflation in the rest of the euro area at 2 percent.

  1. Starting from equation (5) and the growth-rate form of equation (6), show that inside the currency union \(\pi - \pi^w = (1 - \theta)\left[(g_{A_T} - g_{A_N}) - (g_{A^w_T} - g_{A^w_N})\right]\). What is Home’s inflation? How fast do the prices of its traded and its nontraded goods grow?

  2. Before joining, Home still has its own currency, and its central bank keeps Home’s inflation at 2 percent. How must its nominal exchange rate, in euros per unit of Home’s currency, move each year?

  3. To join the euro, a country’s inflation may not exceed that of the three EU members with the lowest inflation by more than 1.5 points (the price-stability criterion). Suppose those three have 1 percent inflation. Can Home pass with a fixed exchange rate against the euro? What is its way out, and what happens after it joins? With one nominal interest rate for the whole union, what does Home’s inflation do to its real interest rate?

  4. The table shows four economies that adopted the euro after 2008. Do the numbers fit the model? Name one other reason why prices in these economies could rise faster than in Germany.

Economy Uses the euro since Inflation minus euro-area inflation, adoption year to 2023 (points a year) Price level relative to Germany, year before adoption Price level relative to Germany, 2023
Slovakia 2009 0.95 0.73 0.84
Estonia 2011 1.85 0.72 0.90
Latvia 2014 1.69 0.69 0.73
Lithuania 2015 2.41 0.63 0.76

Computed from this chapter’s inflation_wdi.csv (World Bank, FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG) and rer_pwt.csv (Penn World Table 11.0, price levels of GDP), with the euro adoption years of countries.csv.

Hint

Inside a currency union the nominal exchange rate never moves, \(g_E = 0\), so equation (5) turns into a statement about the inflation gap. For the prices of the two goods: traded goods obey the law of one price, and \(P_N = P_T A_T/A_N\) (step 1 of the Balassa-Samuelson block) gives the growth of \(P_N\). For (b), keep \(\pi = \pi^w = 2\) and solve equation (5) for \(g_E\).

Your answer:

Solution

(a) Equation (5) says \(g_{RER} \approx g_E + \pi - \pi^w\). In the union \(g_E = 0\), so \(g_{RER} = \pi - \pi^w\). The growth-rate form of equation (6) says \(g_{RER} = (1 - \theta)\left[(g_{A_T} - g_{A_N}) - (g_{A^w_T} - g_{A^w_N})\right]\). The two expressions are the same \(g_{RER}\), so

\[\pi - \pi^w = (1 - \theta)\left[(g_{A_T} - g_{A_N}) - (g_{A^w_T} - g_{A^w_N})\right] = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[(5 - 1) - (2 - 1)\right] = 1.5 \text{ points},\]

and Home’s inflation is \(2 + 1.5 = 3.5\) percent. To find the two prices, use \(P_N = P_T A_T/A_N\) in growth rates: \(\pi_N = \pi_T + g_{A_T} - g_{A_N}\). Abroad, \(\pi^w = \theta\pi_T + (1 - \theta)(\pi_T + 1) = \pi_T + 0.5 = 2\), so traded goods get 1.5 percent dearer a year, in Home as everywhere else (the law of one price). In Home nontraded prices then grow by \(1.5 + 4 = 5.5\) percent, and \(\pi = \tfrac{1}{2}\times 1.5 + \tfrac{1}{2}\times 5.5 = 3.5\) percent. Home’s higher inflation is all in haircuts and restaurant meals: its fast factories raise wages everywhere.

(b) With \(\pi = \pi^w = 2\), equation (5) gives \(g_E = g_{RER} - \pi + \pi^w = 1.5 - 2 + 2 = 1.5\) percent a year. Home’s currency must appreciate by 1.5 percent a year in nominal terms. The real appreciation of Home that its catching up requires comes through the exchange rate instead of through inflation.

(c) The reference value is \(1 + 1.5 = 2.5\) percent. With a fixed exchange rate, Home’s inflation is 3.5 percent and it fails by a point, although nothing is wrong with its central bank: rising service prices are the normal sign of an economy that catches up. Its way out is the route of (b): keep inflation at 2 percent and let its currency appreciate. The criterion on exchange-rate stability forbids devaluations, not appreciations. But once Home is inside, \(g_E = 0\) again and inflation returns to 3.5 percent; the criterion only postpones it. With one nominal rate \(i\) for the whole union, Home’s real rate \(R = i - \pi\) is then 1.5 points lower than in the rest of the union, which encourages borrowing. This is one road to the credit booms of Fig. 10.

(d) The numbers fit the direction of the model. All four economies had inflation 0.95 to 2.41 points a year above the euro area after they adopted the euro, and all four price levels rose relative to Germany’s, Estonia’s from 0.72 to 0.90. Inside a union the two columns should match, since \(g_{RER} = \pi - \pi^w\): the price level relative to Germany grew by 1.01 percent a year in Slovakia, 1.80 in Estonia, 0.56 in Latvia and 1.94 in Lithuania. That is close to the inflation gaps for Slovakia and Estonia, but not for Latvia and Lithuania; the two columns also use different price indexes, consumer prices for inflation and GDP prices for the price levels. Another reason: a demand boom. By (c), the same nominal rate means a lower real rate where inflation is higher, so households borrow and spend more, and the prices of nontraded goods rise without any gain in productivity. Southern Europe saw such booms before 2008 (Figs. 10 and 11).

Data-based problems

Problem 4 (Basic): Which currencies are pegged? A fixed exchange rate should hardly change from one year to the next. Use the end-of-year exchange rates against the dollar of the IMF’s Exchange Rates dataset, in fx_crises.csv (the file of Fig. 8).

  1. For each economy, compute the yearly percent changes of its exchange rate from the end of 2010 to the end of 2025, and their standard deviation, the typical yearly change, as in the Key numbers of Fig. 6. Keep the economies that have all 15 changes. How many never changed their rate at all? Which one of them should you leave out, and why?

  2. Which economies have a typical change above zero but below 0.5 percent?

  3. Denmark’s typical change against the dollar is about as large as the euro’s. Compute Denmark’s exchange rate against the euro instead (kroner per euro = kroner per dollar ÷ euros per dollar) and its typical yearly change. What do you conclude?

Hint

groupby("country").per_usd_eop.pct_change() computes the changes country by country (sort the rows by country and year first), and .agg(["std", "count"]) gives the standard deviation and the number of changes of each country. For (c), take the Denmark and the Euro area rows, use set_index("year"), and divide one series by the other.

# Your answer here
Solution

Keep the years 2010 to 2025, compute each economy’s percent changes, then their standard deviation and count.

ends = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fx_crises.csv")
recent = ends[(ends.year >= 2010) & (ends.year <= 2025)].sort_values(["country", "year"]).copy()
recent["change"] = 100 * recent.groupby("country").per_usd_eop.pct_change()
volatility = recent.groupby("country").change.agg(["std", "count"])
volatility = volatility[volatility["count"] == 15].sort_values("std")
never = volatility[volatility["std"] == 0].index
print(len(volatility), "economies with all 15 changes;", len(never), "never changed their rate:")
print(", ".join(never))
print(volatility[(volatility["std"] > 0) & (volatility["std"] < 0.5)].round(2))

(a) Of the 164 economies with all 15 changes, 30 kept exactly the same end-of-year rate every year. Leave out the United States: one dollar always costs one dollar, so its row says nothing about a policy. Among the other 29 are five Gulf states (Saudi Arabia at 3.75 riyals, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain), Jordan, Djibouti and many Caribbean economies. Eight of them record exactly 1.0 per dollar every year (Ecuador, El Salvador, Panama, Timor-Leste, Micronesia, Palau, the Bahamas and Bermuda): a rate of exactly one suggests that they use the U.S. dollar itself or a currency tied one for one to it.

(b) Bolivia (0.30 percent), Guyana (0.34), Hong Kong (0.38) and Macao (0.40). Hong Kong’s rate moves a little inside its band of 7.75 to 7.85 (Problem 2), so its changes are small but not zero.

denmark = ends[ends.country == "Denmark"].set_index("year").per_usd_eop
euro = ends[ends.country == "Euro area"].set_index("year").per_usd_eop
kroner_per_euro = (denmark / euro).loc[2010:2025]
print(f"Kroner per euro: lowest {kroner_per_euro.min():.3f}, highest {kroner_per_euro.max():.3f}")
print(f"Typical yearly change: against the euro {(100 * kroner_per_euro.pct_change()).std():.2f}%, "
      f"against the dollar {volatility.loc['Denmark', 'std']:.2f}% (the euro: {volatility.loc['Euro area', 'std']:.2f}%)")

(c) Against the euro, the krone stayed between 7.421 and 7.500 kroner per euro, with a typical yearly change of only 0.45 percent, against 7.84 percent against the dollar (the euro itself: 7.93 percent). Denmark pegs to the euro, not to the dollar: Danmarks Nationalbank keeps the krone close to 746.038 kroner per 100 euros. A peg is invisible in a table of dollar rates when the anchor currency is not the dollar: always ask pegged to what?

Problem 5 (Intermediate): Does PPP hold for 21 currencies? Equation (4) predicts that, over long periods, a currency loses value against the dollar each year by its inflation gap with the United States. Test it with the monthly exchange rates of the Federal Reserve’s H.10 release in fx_monthly.csv and the World Bank’s consumer-price inflation, FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG, in inflation_wdi.csv.

  1. For every currency with exchange rates in 2000 and 2024 and inflation in all years 2001–2024, compute from annual averages the yearly log change of the price of a dollar, \(g_E = 100\ln(E_{2024}/E_{2000})/24\), and the average gap between its inflation and U.S. inflation over 2001–2024.

  2. Compute the correlation between the two columns and the slope of a straight line through them. What slope does equation (4) predict?

  3. By equation (5), \(g_E\) minus the inflation gap is the yearly change of the dollar’s real exchange rate against that currency. Which three currencies have the largest real change in each direction? Explain the largest one.

  4. Which currency in fx_monthly.csv drops out because it has no inflation data?

Hint

Average each currency’s months with groupby(["country", "year"]).per_usd.mean(); the result is looked up with a pair, e.g. yearly[("Japan", 2024)]. Then loop over the countries and collect one dictionary per currency, as period_means does for Fig. 11. np.polyfit(x, y, 1)[0] is the slope of the best straight line.

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution 
monthly = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fx_monthly.csv")
monthly["year"] = monthly.date.str[:4].astype(int)
yearly = monthly.groupby(["country", "year"]).per_usd.mean()       # annual averages
cpi = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "inflation_wdi.csv")
us_mean = cpi[(cpi.country == "United States") & (cpi.year >= 2001) & (cpi.year <= 2024)].inflation.mean()
rows = []
for name in sorted(monthly.country.unique()):
    own = cpi[(cpi.country == name) & (cpi.year >= 2001) & (cpi.year <= 2024)]
    if (name, 2000) in yearly.index and (name, 2024) in yearly.index and len(own) == 24:
        g_E = 100 * np.log(yearly[(name, 2024)] / yearly[(name, 2000)]) / 24
        rows.append({"country": name, "g_E": g_E, "gap": own.inflation.mean() - us_mean})
ppp = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("country")
ppp["real"] = ppp.g_E - ppp.gap                                    # equation (5)
print(len(ppp), "currencies; correlation", round(ppp.g_E.corr(ppp.gap), 2),
      "; slope", round(np.polyfit(ppp.gap, ppp.g_E, 1)[0], 2))
print(ppp.sort_values("real").round(2).iloc[[0, 1, 2, -3, -2, -1]])

(a)–(b) 21 currencies qualify. The correlation between \(g_E\) and the inflation gap is 0.86 and the slope is 0.83. Equation (4) predicts a slope of one: each extra point of inflation should cost a currency one point of value against the dollar a year. The data come close. Sri Lanka, Brazil, South Africa, India and Mexico had the most inflation, and the dollar bought 2.6 to 5.7 percent more of their currencies each year; the Swiss franc and the yen had the least. PPP is a good guide to the long run, but not an exact law.

(c) The dollar’s real exchange rate fell most against the Sri Lankan rupee (−1.42 percent a year), the New Zealand dollar (−1.21) and the Indian rupee (−1.05): their goods got dearer relative to U.S. goods. It rose most against the Malaysian ringgit (+1.20), the South African rand (+1.35) and, by far, the yen (+3.50 percent a year). Japan had 2.08 points less inflation than the United States, yet the dollar bought 1.42 percent more yen each year, so Japanese goods became about 3.5 percent a year cheaper relative to U.S. goods: the fall of Japan’s real exchange rate after 1995 in Fig. 3. Low Japanese interest rates are one reason (Problem 7).

(d) Taiwan: it has no rows in the World Bank file. The mark, the franc and the lira drop out too, because they stop in 2001.

Problem 6 (Intermediate): What predicted the euro-crisis spreads? Two kinds of borrowing grew in the euro area before 2008: borrowing by governments (Fig. 12) and borrowing by whole economies from abroad (Fig. 11). Which one better predicts the bond spreads of 2010–2012? Use the 10-year yields in yields_monthly.csv (OECD data via FRED, and Eurostat for Cyprus and Malta), the IMF’s government debt in debt.csv (GGXWDG_NGDP), the IMF’s current account balances in current_account_imf.csv (BCA_NGDPD), and the column euro_since of countries.csv.

  1. For every country that used the euro by 2009, except Germany, find its largest monthly spread over Germany from January 2010 to December 2012, its IMF government debt in 2009 (percent of GDP), and its average current account balance in 2003–2007.

  2. Compute the correlation of the peak spread with each of the two other columns. Then leave out Greece and compute them again.

  3. Which kind of borrowing was the better warning sign? Name a pair of countries that shows it.

  4. Use equation (14) to turn Portugal’s peak spread into a yearly probability of default, first with the approximation and then exactly.

Hint

Take Germany’s yields with set_index("date")["yield"]; the spread of another country is its series minus Germany’s, and .loc["2010-01":"2012-12"] keeps the crisis years. Collect one dictionary per country in a loop, and use .corr() on the resulting table. For the exact answer in (d), solve \((1 - p)(1 + i) = 1 + i^{safe}\) for \(p\), with the two yields of the peak month.

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution 
bonds = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "yields_monthly.csv")
debts = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "debt.csv")
accounts = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "current_account_imf.csv")
members = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")
early = members[(members.euro_since <= 2009) & (members.country != "Germany")].country
german = bonds[bonds.country == "Germany"].set_index("date")["yield"]
rows = []
for name in early:
    own = bonds[bonds.country == name].set_index("date")["yield"]
    spread = (own - german).loc["2010-01":"2012-12"]
    debt09 = debts[(debts.country == name) & (debts.year == 2009)].debt_imf.iloc[0]
    boom = accounts[(accounts.country == name) & (accounts.year >= 2003) & (accounts.year <= 2007)]
    rows.append({"country": name, "peak_spread": spread.max(), "debt_2009": debt09,
                 "ca_2003_07": boom.ca_gdp.mean()})
euro_crisis = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("country").sort_values("peak_spread")
print(euro_crisis.round(1))
print("all:", euro_crisis.corr().round(2).loc["peak_spread", ["debt_2009", "ca_2003_07"]].to_dict())
no_greece = euro_crisis.drop("Greece")
print("without Greece:", no_greece.corr().round(2).loc["peak_spread", ["debt_2009", "ca_2003_07"]].to_dict())

(a)–(b) Fifteen countries qualify. Peak spreads run from 0.6 points (Luxembourg) to 27.4 points (Greece, February 2012). The correlation of the peak spread with government debt in 2009 is 0.57, and with the current account of 2003–2007 it is −0.66. Without Greece, which had both the most debt and the largest deficit, the correlation with debt falls to 0.25, while the one with the current account strengthens to −0.74.

(c) The current account, the borrowing of the whole economy from abroad, was the better warning sign. Compare Belgium and Spain: Belgium’s government debt was 99.9 percent of GDP in 2009, Spain’s only 53.1 percent, but Belgium had run a surplus of 2.4 percent of GDP in 2003–2007 and Spain a deficit of 6.9 percent, and Spain’s peak spread (5.6 points) was almost twice Belgium’s (3.0). Cyprus and Slovakia, with modest debts and large deficits, tell the same story. Much of the foreign borrowing went through private banks (Fig. 10), and when the banks got into trouble their debts became their governments’ problem: Ireland’s debt jumped after 2008 (Fig. 12).

(d) Portugal’s peak spread was 12.03 points, in January 2012, so the approximation \(i \approx i^{safe} + p\) gives a default probability of about 12 percent a year. Exactly, with Portugal’s yield of 13.85 percent and Germany’s 1.821 percent: \(p = 1 - (1 + i^{safe})/(1 + i) = 1 - 1.01821/1.1385 = 0.1057\), or 10.57 percent a year. Markets priced a roughly one-in-ten chance of default each year; the approximation overstates it, because the yields are not small.

portugal = bonds[bonds.country == "Portugal"].set_index("date")["yield"]
month = (portugal - german).loc["2010-01":"2012-12"].idxmax()
p = 1 - (1 + german[month] / 100) / (1 + portugal[month] / 100)      # equation (14), exact
print(f"{month}: Portugal {portugal[month]:.2f}%, Germany {german[month]:.3f}%, default probability {100 * p:.2f}%")

Problem 7 (Challenge): Do interest rates explain the weak yen? Equation (8) says that, with the anchor \(E^e_{t+n}\) held fixed, each point of interest gap expected to last \(n\) years raises today’s exchange rate by about \(n\) percent. Apply it to 10-year government bonds, using the yields of the OECD via FRED in yields_monthly.csv (United States, Japan) and the yen per dollar in fx_monthly.csv.

  1. Show that uncovered interest parity for a 10-year bond gives equation (8) with \(n = 10\): one point more in the gap between U.S. and Japanese 10-year yields should raise the price of a dollar in yen by about 10 percent.

  2. Compute the yield gap and the yen per dollar in January 2021 and October 2022. Compare the change in \(100\ln E\) with 10 times the change in the gap. Then do the same from January 2025 to July 2026, the month in which a dollar bought the most yen since 1986 (Fig. 1).

  3. In the second period the gap shrank, but the yen did not get stronger. Compute Japan’s average inflation in 2001–2021 and in 2022–2025. Use the Fisher equation, \(i = R + \pi^e\), and PPP, equation (4), to explain why a rise in Japanese yields that only reflects higher expected Japanese inflation need not strengthen the yen. Which assumption of the UIP block fails?

Hint

For (a), follow step 1 of the UIP block over 10 years: one dollar grows to \((1 + i)^{10}\) dollars at home, or to \(E_t(1 + i^w)^{10}/E^e_{t+10}\) dollars abroad. For (b), select each series with set_index("date") and read a month with ["2021-01"]. For (c), ask how a higher \(\pi^{e,w}\) changes both \(i^w\) and the anchor \(E^e_{t+10}\).

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution

(a) An investor can hold a U.S. 10-year bond, and have \((1 + i)^{10}\) dollars after 10 years, or a Japanese one, and have \(E_t(1 + i^w)^{10}/E^e_{t+10}\) dollars. If the two must pay the same,

\[(1 + i)^{10} = (1 + i^w)^{10}\,\frac{E_t}{E^e_{t+10}} \;\Longrightarrow\; \ln E_t = \ln E^e_{t+10} + 10\left[\ln(1 + i) - \ln(1 + i^w)\right] \approx \ln E^e_{t+10} + 10\,(i - i^w),\]

which is equation (8) with \(n = 10\). With the anchor fixed, a rise of one point in \(i - i^w\) raises \(\ln E_t\) by 0.10, about 10 percent.

bonds = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "yields_monthly.csv")
monthly = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fx_monthly.csv")
us_yield = bonds[bonds.country == "United States"].set_index("date")["yield"]
jp_yield = bonds[bonds.country == "Japan"].set_index("date")["yield"]
yen_rate = monthly[monthly.country == "Japan"].set_index("date").per_usd
for first, last in [("2021-01", "2022-10"), ("2025-01", "2026-07")]:
    gap_first = us_yield[first] - jp_yield[first]
    gap_last = us_yield[last] - jp_yield[last]
    predicted = 10 * (gap_last - gap_first)                # equation (8) with n = 10
    actual = 100 * np.log(yen_rate[last] / yen_rate[first])
    print(f"{first} to {last}: gap {gap_first:.2f} -> {gap_last:.2f} points, yen {yen_rate[first]:.1f} -> "
          f"{yen_rate[last]:.1f}; predicted {predicted:+.1f}%, actual {actual:+.1f}%")
cpi = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "inflation_wdi.csv")
japan = cpi[cpi.country == "Japan"].set_index("year").inflation
print(f"Japanese inflation: {japan.loc[2001:2021].mean():.2f}% a year in 2001-2021, "
      f"{japan.loc[2022:2025].mean():.2f}% in 2022-2025")

(b) From January 2021 to October 2022 the gap widened from 1.03 to 3.73 points, as U.S. yields rose and Japan’s stayed near zero. Equation (8) predicts a rise of 27.1 percent in the price of a dollar; the actual rise, from 103.8 to 147.1 yen, was 34.8 percent. UIP explains about four fifths of the yen’s fall. From January 2025 to July 2026 the gap shrank from 3.38 to 1.81 points, so equation (8) predicts a fall of 15.8 percent in the price of a dollar, but the dollar went from 156.5 to 162.3 yen, a rise of 3.7 percent. Here UIP with a fixed anchor gets even the sign wrong.

(c) Japanese inflation averaged 0.12 percent a year in 2001–2021 and 2.92 percent in 2022–2025. Suppose investors now expect Japanese inflation to be higher by \(\Delta\) points for the next 10 years, with the real rates unchanged. By the Fisher equation, the Japanese yield \(i^w\) rises by \(\Delta\), so the gap falls by \(\Delta\), and with a fixed anchor \(\ln E_t\) would fall by \(10\Delta\). But by PPP, equation (4), the yen is now expected to lose \(\Delta\) percent more a year against the dollar, so the anchor \(\ln E^e_{t+10}\) rises by \(10\Delta\). The two effects cancel:

\[\Delta \ln E_t = \Delta \ln E^e_{t+10} + 10\,\Delta(i - i^w) = 10\Delta - 10\Delta = 0.\]

Only a change in the real interest gap moves the exchange rate today. Assumption 3 of the UIP block, a fixed anchor, fails whenever expected inflation changes. If the rise in Japanese yields after 2024 mostly reflected Japan’s higher inflation, the narrower nominal gap did not mean a narrower real gap, and the yen had no reason to recover. The model also ignores risk (assumption 2), which can move exchange rates on its own.

Modeling problems

Problem 8 (Basic): How high must the central bank go? The central bank of an open economy wants to lower short-run output by 3 percent, starting from potential output at \(R = \bar{r} = 5\) percent (for example, to bring inflation down). Use the IS diagram of Fig. 4 below; the investment sensitivity stays at \(\bar{b}_i = 1\). (The cell below wraps tightening in a small function that shows its readout with two decimals.)

  1. With the baseline trade channel, \(\bar{b}_{nx} = 1\), what real interest rate must the central bank set? How much of the fall in output comes through net exports?

  2. What rate would it need in a closed economy, \(\bar{b}_{nx} = 0\)? And if net exports react only half as strongly as in the baseline, \(\bar{b}_{nx} = 0.5\)?

  3. Derive the general rule: the rate \(R'\) that lowers output by \(x\) percent. Why does a more open economy need a smaller change in its interest rate?

Hint

Move the rate slider until the title shows \(\tilde{Y}' = -3.00\) percent; the title also splits the fall between investment and net exports. For (c), set \(\bar{a} = 0\) in equation (11) and solve for \(R\).

def tightening_two_decimals(R_new=6.0, b_nx=B_NX):
    """Fig. 4 with b_i = 1, and its readout to two decimals for the half-point steps of b_nx."""
    fig = tightening(R_new, b_nx, B_I)
    invest = -B_I * (R_new - R_BAR) + 0.0                  # + 0.0 avoids printing -0.0
    trade = -b_nx * (R_new - R_BAR) + 0.0
    fig.update_layout(title=f"R′ = {R_new:.2f}%  →  Ỹ′ = {invest + trade + 0.0:.2f}%   "
                            f"(investment {invest:.2f}, net exports {trade:.2f})")
    return fig


interact(tightening_two_decimals,
         R_new=FloatSlider(value=6.0, min=5.0, max=8.0, step=0.5, description="new real interest rate R′ (%)", style=WIDE),
         b_nx=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.0, max=2.0, step=0.5, description="net-export sensitivity b̄ₙₓ", style=WIDE));

Source. The model of Fig. 4 above, adapted from Fig. 20.4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution

(c) first, the rule. With \(\bar{a} = 0\), equation (11) is \(\tilde{Y} = -(\bar{b}_i + \bar{b}_{nx})(R - \bar{r})\). Set \(\tilde{Y} = -x\) and solve:

\[R' = \bar{r} + \frac{x}{\bar{b}_i + \bar{b}_{nx}}.\]

(a) \(R' = 5 + 3/(1 + 1) = 6.5\) percent. The title splits the fall into −1.50 points through investment and −1.50 points through net exports: half of the fall comes through net exports, because \(\bar{b}_{nx}\) is half of \(\bar{b}\).

(b) Closed economy: \(R' = 5 + 3/1 = 8.0\) percent, a rise of 3 points instead of 1.5. With \(\bar{b}_{nx} = 0.5\): \(R' = 5 + 3/1.5 = 7.0\) percent.

for b_nx in [1.0, 0.0, 0.5]:
    R_needed = R_BAR + 3 / (B_I + b_nx)                   # the rule, from equation (11) with a = 0
    print(f"b_nx = {b_nx}: R' = {R_needed:.2f}%, output {is_curve(R_needed, b_nx=b_nx):+.1f}%, "
          f"of which net exports {net_exports(R_needed, b_nx=b_nx):+.2f} points")

Interpretation. In an open economy a higher interest rate works through two channels. It makes investment more expensive, and by uncovered interest parity it makes the currency appreciate, which makes the country’s goods dearer abroad and lowers net exports. The larger \(\bar{b}_{nx}\), the flatter the IS curve and the smaller the rate change the central bank needs. The flip side is that part of the cooling falls on the country’s trading partners: they now sell more to it and buy less from it.

Problem 9 (Intermediate): A firmer Fed against a foreign shock. The ECB raises its real interest rate 2 points above \(\bar{r}\) for nine periods, as in Fig. 5. The Fed wants U.S. inflation to stay below 3.5 percent the whole time.

  1. With the sliders, find the smallest policy response \(\bar{m}\) (in steps of 0.25) that keeps inflation below 3.5 percent. In which period does inflation peak?

  2. Compare the boom in period 1 and the recession in period 10 at \(\bar{m} = 0.5\) and at your answer to (a). Confirm the numbers with simulate.

  3. Here a firmer response makes both the boom and the recession smaller. Explain why with equation (13). Why is this not true for an inflation shock, a shock to the Phillips curve as in Chapter 13?

Hint

For each value of \(\bar{m}\), move the period slider and watch inflation in the title: when does it stop rising? Then look at periods 1 and 10. In equation (13), see where \(\bar{m}\) appears in the numerator and in the denominator.

interact(foreign_rate_shock,
         gap=fixed(2.0),
         t=IntSlider(value=9, min=1, max=20, step=1, description="period t", style=WIDE),
         b_nx=fixed(1.0),
         m=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.5, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE));

Source. The model of Fig. 5 above, adapted from Fig. 20.5 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution

(a) At \(\bar{m} = 0.5\) inflation reaches 4.00 percent in period 9. At \(\bar{m} = 0.75\) it peaks at 3.33 percent, also in period 9, the last period of the shock. So \(\bar{m} = 0.75\) is the smallest response that keeps inflation below 3.5 percent.

(b) At \(\bar{m} = 0.5\) output is 1.00 percent above potential in period 1 and 1.00 percent below it in period 10. At \(\bar{m} = 0.75\) the boom is 0.80 percent and the recession 0.80 percent.

shock = foreign_shock(R_BAR + 2.0)                         # a = 2 in periods 1 to 9
for m in [0.5, 0.75]:
    path = simulate(shock_list(shock), m=m)
    peak = path.pi.idxmax()
    print(f"m = {m}: peak inflation {path.pi.max():.2f}% in period {path.period[peak]}, "
          f"Y~ {path.Y[1]:+.2f}% in period 1 and {path.Y[10]:+.2f}% in period 10")

(c) In period 1, equation (13) gives \(\tilde{Y}_1 = \bar{a}/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\): a larger \(\bar{m}\) raises the denominator, because the Fed raises U.S. rates as soon as inflation moves, which offsets part of the boom in net exports. While the shock lasts, inflation heads for \(\bar{\pi} + \bar{a}/(\bar{b}\bar{m})\), which is lower when \(\bar{m}\) is larger, so there is less inflation to unwind when the shock ends. In period 10, with \(\bar{a} = 0\) and inflation close to that resting point, equation (13) gives \(\tilde{Y}_{10} \approx -\bar{b}\bar{m}\,\big(\bar{a}/(\bar{b}\bar{m})\big)/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}) = -\bar{a}/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\), again smaller for a larger \(\bar{m}\): \(-2/2 = -1\) at \(\bar{m} = 0.5\) and \(-2/2.5 = -0.8\) at \(\bar{m} = 0.75\). A demand shock pushes output and inflation in the same direction, so fighting inflation also steadies output: there is no trade-off. A shock to the Phillips curve pushes inflation up while output falls; then a firmer response brings inflation down faster, but only with a deeper recession.

Problem 10 (Challenge): The euro in 2022, on the trilemma. In 2022 the Fed raised its target range by 4.25 points, from 0–0.25 to 4.25–4.50 percent, while the ECB raised its deposit facility rate by 2.5 points, from −0.50 to 2.00 percent. Treat the euro area as “your economy” in the trilemma model of Fig. 7, and the United States as the foreign country. (The cell below wraps trilemma in a small function that shows its readout with two decimals, since the sliders move in quarter points.)

  1. Choose the floating regime, and set the foreign rate rise to 4.25 points and the euro area’s own change to 2.5 points. What does the model predict for the euro’s value in dollars?

  2. From fig20-1.csv (the Federal Reserve’s H.10 data of Fig. 1), compute the dollars per euro, 1 / eur_per_usd, in December 2021 and in December 2022, and the percent change. What value of \(\eta\), the model’s percent change in \(E\) per point of interest gap, would match the data? By step 2 of the UIP block, what does that \(\eta\) say about how long investors expected the gap to last?

  3. Find the euro’s lowest month in 2022. On the same two pages, look at how each central bank moved its rate in 2023, and suggest why the euro recovered at the end of 2022.

  4. Policy: suppose the euro area had pegged its currency to the dollar. Switch to the currency board. What rate change would the ECB have needed? Name a gain and a cost, knowing that in 2023 real GDP grew by 0.4 percent in the euro area and 2.9 percent in the United States.

Hint

In the floating regime the model sets \(\%\Delta E = \eta\,(\Delta i - \Delta i^w)\) with \(\eta = 5\). For (b), solve the same equation for \(\eta\) with the actual change. For (c), equation (8) depends on the interest gap investors expect over the next years, not only on today’s gap.

def trilemma_two_decimals(regime="floating exchange rate", di_world=1.0, di_need=0.0):
    """Fig. 7 with its readout to two decimals, for sliders that move in quarter points."""
    fig = trilemma(regime, di_world, di_need)
    di, dE, lost = trilemma_outcome(regime, di_world, di_need)
    flows = "blocked" if regime == "capital controls" else "free"
    fig.layout.annotations[-1].text = (f"Interest rate: {di:+.2f} pt<br>Exchange rate: {dE:+.2f}%<br>"
                                       f"Capital flows: {flows}")                  # the readout box
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{regime.capitalize()}: Δi = {di:+.2f}, %ΔE = {dE:+.2f}; lost: {lost}")
    return fig


interact(trilemma_two_decimals,
         regime=ToggleButtons(options=["floating exchange rate", "currency board", "capital controls"],
                              value="floating exchange rate", description="regime", style=WIDE),
         di_world=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.0, max=5.0, step=0.25, description="Fed's rate rise Δiʷ (points)", style=WIDE),
         di_need=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=0.0, max=5.0, step=0.25, description="euro area's own change (points)", style=WIDE));

Source. The model of Fig. 7 above, adapted from Fig. 20.7 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here

Your answer:

Solution

(a) The readout box shows an interest-rate change of +2.50 points and an exchange-rate change of −8.75 percent. The model predicts that the euro’s dollar value changes by \(5 \times (2.5 - 4.25) = -8.75\) percent, because U.S. rates rose 1.75 points more than euro rates. The goal given up is a stable exchange rate.

rates = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig20-1.csv", parse_dates=["date"]).set_index("date")
dollars_per_euro = 1 / rates.eur_per_usd
before, after = dollars_per_euro["2021-12-01"], dollars_per_euro["2022-12-01"]
change = 100 * (after / before - 1)
print(f"Dollars per euro: {before:.4f} in Dec 2021, {after:.4f} in Dec 2022, a change of {change:+.2f}%")
model = trilemma_outcome("floating exchange rate", 4.25, 2.5)[1]
print(f"Model: {model:+.2f}%; the eta that matches the data: {-change / (4.25 - 2.5):.2f}")
low = dollars_per_euro.loc["2022-01-01":"2022-12-01"]
print(f"Lowest month of 2022: {low.idxmin().strftime('%Y-%m')}, {low.min():.4f} dollars per euro, "
      f"{100 * (low.min() / before - 1):+.1f}% since Dec 2021")

(b) A euro bought 1.1301 dollars in December 2021 and 1.0591 in December 2022, a fall of 6.28 percent. The model, with \(\eta = 5\), predicted −8.75 percent; the data match \(\eta = 6.28/1.75 = 3.59\). By step 2 of the UIP block, \(\eta\) is the number of years \(n\) that the gap is expected to last, so investors acted as if the extra 1.75 points of U.S. interest would last about three and a half years.

(c) The euro’s lowest month was October 2022, at 0.9853 dollars, 12.8 percent below December 2021. In 2023 the ECB raised its deposit rate by another 2 points, to 4.00 percent, while the Fed added only 1 point, to 5.25–5.50 percent. One explanation: if investors came to expect this narrowing at the end of 2022, the gap they expected over the next years fell, and by equation (8) the euro rose again before most of those increases actually happened.

(d) With a currency board the ECB would have had to match the Fed: \(\Delta i = +4.25\) points, 1.75 more than it chose, with no change in the exchange rate. Gain: no depreciation, so no extra rise in the euro prices of imports paid in dollars at a time of high inflation. Cost: a tighter policy than the ECB judged right for the euro area, which grew by only 0.4 percent in 2023, against 2.9 percent in the United States. A floating rate let each central bank choose for its own economy; that is the trilemma’s lesson for large economies.
